After a big small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they need a long, normal trip through the gut to release the drug.

why.claim: This is a regular tablet that releases right away, not a timed-release or coated one.
Timed-release and coated medicines are usually avoided after a large part of the small bowel is removed. This tablet is not that kind.
Plain fast-dissolving tablets are in the lowest-risk group for dissolving problems in people with a stoma.
Most medicines are absorbed in the first part of the small bowel, so many plain tablets can still be absorbed when that part remains.
How well a medicine is absorbed depends mostly on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is. You have under 100 cm.
In studies, 29 of 37 drugs were absorbed less after bowel surgery, and 6 stopped working. It differs from drug to drug, so it can't be predicted for one person.
For some drugs, doctors may check blood levels or watch the effect closely, because absorption after surgery is hard to predict.
The label says food and antacids don't change how it is absorbed.
The label lists croscarmellose sodium and hydrogenated vegetable oil as extra ingredients. No sorbitol is listed.

How well pills are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

why.claim: The label I matched for this medicine (RELEXXII, a methylphenidate extended-release tablet) lists it as an extended-release tablet.

Liquid medicines can absorb more reliably, but they often contain sugar alcohols that can increase stoma output.

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask if this medicine comes in a form from the study's lower-risk group, such as a solution or a plain tablet that dissolves fast.

draft.verdict: Protonix is a delayed-release, enteric-coated tablet, and short bowel guidelines flag this kind of coating as one that may not dissolve in time after bowel surgery, so it's worth checking with your pharmacist whether it will work for your body.

why.claim: Protonix tablets are delayed-release.
The tablet has an enteric coating, so the medicine only starts to absorb after the tablet leaves the stomach.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, delayed-release and enteric-coated medicines are generally avoided. They need a long, normal trip through the gut to release the drug.
When things move through the gut fast, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets come out whole.
One study of people with an ostomy put enteric-coated products in its highest-risk group for not dissolving.
How well a pill absorbs depends more on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is than on the type of stoma. You have 100 to 200 cm, so your team can judge this for you.
Acid-lowering medicines are often used to reduce output after major bowel surgery. Still, the form of the pill matters for absorption.
The tablet also contains mannitol as an inactive ingredient.
Mannitol and other sugar alcohols pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output.
The label says not to split, crush, or chew Protonix tablets or the Protonix suspension. Whether a different form makes sense is a decision for your pharmacist or prescriber.
Of 15 people with an ileostomy who logged this medicine, 2 said it helped, 8 noticed no change, and 5 said it caused problems.

final.verdict: Protonix is a delayed-release, enteric-coated tablet, and short bowel guidelines flag this kind of coating as one that may not dissolve in time when the gut moves fast after bowel surgery, so it's worth checking with your pharmacist whether it can be absorbed in your body.

why.claim: Protonix tablets are delayed-release.
The tablet has an enteric coating, so the medicine only starts to absorb after the tablet leaves the stomach.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, delayed-release and enteric-coated medicines are generally avoided. They need a long, normal trip through the gut to release the drug.
When things move through the gut fast, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets come out whole.
One study of people with an ostomy put enteric-coated products in its highest-risk group for not dissolving.
How well a pill absorbs depends more on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is than on the type of stoma.
Acid-lowering medicines are often used to reduce output after major bowel surgery. Still, the form of the pill matters for absorption.
The tablet also contains mannitol as an inactive ingredient.
Mannitol and other sugar alcohols pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output.
The label says not to split, crush, or chew Protonix tablets or the Protonix suspension. Whether a different form makes sense is a decision for your pharmacist or prescriber.
Of 15 people with an ileostomy who logged this medicine, 2 said it helped, 8 noticed no change, and 5 said it caused problems.

draft.ask: ASK: With my ileostomy and 100 to 200 cm of small bowel, could this spironolactone suspension raise my risk of dehydration or low sodium?
sourcesChecked: Guidelines: liquid medicine absorption in short bowel / ileostomy
Guidelines: diuretics and dehydration with ileostomy
draft.verdict: The liquid form may suit your body, but two things are worth checking with your pharmacist: the full ingredient list was missing, and guidelines warn that diuretics can raise dehydration risk with an ileostomy.

why.claim: This product is a suspension, which is a liquid.
In short bowel syndrome, liquid medicines may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets. But liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols, which can increase output.
Sugar alcohols like sorbitol draw water into the gut and can raise stoma output. They are common inactive ingredients in liquid medicines.

The label part I found only starts the list of inactive ingredients (sorbic acid, potassium sorbate, citric acid anhydrous...). The full inactive ingredient section was missing, so I could not confirm whether it has sugar alcohols. Sorbic acid is a different thing from sorbitol.
People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium. Medicines such as diuretics can add to that risk.
Warning signs of dehydration include thirst, dark or reduced urine, dizziness when standing, and rising stoma output. Tell your care team promptly if you notice them.
How well a medicine taken by mouth is absorbed depends more on the length and health of the remaining small bowel than on the type of stoma.
The label says a high-fat, high-calorie meal raised how much spironolactone the body took in by about 90%. So timing with meals can change how much you absorb.

why.claim: This product is an extended-release tablet.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, slow-release and coated medicines are generally avoided. They need a long, normal trip through the gut to let the drug out.
With a shorter bowel or faster transit, part of a slow-release dose may leave the body before it is let out.
The label says the potassium chloride in these tablets is fully absorbed before it leaves the small intestine. That label statement does not describe a shortened bowel.
The label says to swallow the tablets whole, without crushing, chewing or sucking. Whether a different form would suit you is a decision for your pharmacist or prescriber.
How well pills absorb depends more on how long and healthy your remaining small bowel is than on the type of surgery.
Liquid medicines can absorb more reliably than tablets in short bowel syndrome. But liquids often contain sugar alcohols, which can raise output.
Of 13 people with small bowel joined to colon who logged this, 2 said it helped, 9 noticed no change, and 2 said it made things worse.

why.claim: The label lists sorbitol solution as one of the ingredients in Carafate Oral Suspension.

The product is a suspension, which is a liquid.
Solutions are grouped as low-risk for dissolving problems in people with an ostomy.
The label says very little sucralfate is absorbed from the gut, so how much your bowel absorbs is not the main question for this medicine.

why.claim: Depakote tablets are delayed-release tablets.
The label says Depakote tablets should be swallowed whole and should not be crushed or chewed.
The Depakote Sprinkle capsules are also described as delayed-release capsules.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, delayed-release and coated medicines are usually avoided, because they need a long, normal gut to release the drug.
Coated and delayed-release pills are made to dissolve after the stomach. If food moves through fast, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some pills come out whole.
How well pills are absorbed depends mostly on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is. Your small-bowel length is not known, so it is hard to say how much this applies to you.
Studies show surgery on the bowel lowered absorption for many drugs, but it differs from drug to drug, so no one can give you an exact chance.
The label says your doctor can check the valproate level in your blood if the medicine is not working well enough.
No one has logged how they did with this medicine, with your anatomy or any other.

evidence.L:boxed_warning: WARNING: LIFE THREATENING ADVERSE REACTIONS Hepatotoxicity General Population: Hepatic failure resulting in fatalities has occurred in patients receiving valproate and its derivatives. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment. Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. Children under the age of two years are at a considerably increased risk of developing fatal hepatotoxicity, especially those on multiple anticonvulsants, those with congenital metabolic disorders, those with severe seizure disorders accompanied by mental retardation, and those with organic brain disease. When Depakote is used in this patient group, it should be used with extreme caution and as a sole agent. The benefits of therapy should be weighed against the risks. The incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases considerably in progressively older patient groups. Patients with Mitochondrial Disease: There is an increased risk of valproate-induced acute liver failure and resultant deaths in patients with hereditary neurometabolic syndromes caused by DNA mutations of the mitochondrial DNA Polymerase γ (POLG) gene (e.g. , Alpers Huttenlocher Syndrome). Depakote is contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder [see Contraindications ( 4 )]. In patients over two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a hereditary mitochondrial disease, Depakote should only be used after other anticonvulsants have failed. This older group of patients should be closely monitored during treatment with Depakote for the development of acute liver injury with regular clinical assessments and serum liver testing. POLG mutation screening should be performed in accordance with current clinical practice [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. Fetal Risk Valproate can cause major congenital malformations, particularly neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida). In addition, valproate can cause decreased IQ scores and neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure. Valproate is therefore contraindicated for prophylaxis of migraine headaches in pregnant women and in women of childbearing potential who are not using effective contraception [see Contraindications ( 4 )]. Valproate should not be used to treat women with epilepsy or bipolar disorder who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. Valproate should not be administered to a woman of childbearing potential unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. In such situations, effective contraception should be used [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 , 5.3 , 5.4 )]. A Medication Guide describing the risks of valproate is available for patients [see Patient Counseling Information ( 17 )]. Pancreatitis Cases of life-threatening pancreatitis have been reported in both children and adults receiving valproate. Some of the cases have been described as hemorrhagic with a rapid progression from initial symptoms to death. Cases have been reported shortly after initial use as well as after several years of use. Patients and guardians should be warned that abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and/or anorexia can be symptoms of pancreatitis that require prompt medical evaluation. evidence.L:clinical_pharmacology: 12 CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY 12.1 Mechanism of Action Divalproex sodium dissociates to the valproate ion in the gastrointestinal tract. The mechanisms by which valproate exerts its therapeutic effects have not been established. It has been suggested that its activity in epilepsy is related to increased brain concentrations of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). 12.2 Pharmacodynamics The relationship between plasma concentration and clinical response is not well documented. One contributing factor is the nonlinear, concentration dependent protein binding of valproate which affects the clearance of the drug. Thus, monitoring of total serum valproate cannot provide a reliable index of the bioactive valproate species. For example, because the plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent, the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Higher than expected free fractions occur in the elderly, in hyperlipidemic patients, and in patients with hepatic and renal diseases. Epilepsy The therapeutic range in epilepsy is commonly considered to be 50 to 100 mcg/mL of total valproate, although some patients may be controlled with lower or higher plasma concentrations. Mania In placebo-controlled clinical trials of acute mania, patients were dosed to clinical response with trough plasma concentrations between 50 and 125 mcg/mL [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.1 ) ] . 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption/Bioavailability Equivalent oral doses of Depakote (divalproex sodium) products and valproic acid capsules deliver equivalent quantities of valproate ion systemically. Although the rate of valproate ion absorption may vary with the formulation administered (liquid, solid, or sprinkle), conditions of use (e.g., fasting or postprandial) and the method of administration (e.g., whether the contents of the capsule are sprinkled on food or the capsule is taken intact), these differences should be of minor clinical importance under the steady state conditions achieved in chronic use in the treatment of epilepsy. However, it is possible that differences among the various valproate products in T max and C max could be important upon initiation of treatment. For example, in single dose studies, the effect of feeding had a greater influence on the rate of absorption of the tablet (increase in T max from 4 to 8 hours) than on the absorption of the sprinkle capsules (increase in T max from 3.3 to 4.8 hours). While the absorption rate from the G.I. tract and fluctuation in valproate plasma concentrations vary with dosing regimen and formulation, the efficacy of valproate as an anticonvulsant in chronic use is unlikely to be affected. Experience employing dosing regimens from once-a-day to four-times-a-day, as well as studies in primate epilepsy models involving constant rate infusion, indicate that total daily systemic bioavailability (extent of absorption) is the primary determinant of seizure control and that differences in the ratios of plasma peak to trough concentrations between valproate formulations are inconsequential from a practical clinical standpoint. Whether or not rate of absorption influences the efficacy of valproate as an antimanic or antimigraine agent is unknown. Co-administration of oral valproate products with food and substitution among the various Depakote and valproic acid formulations should cause no clinical problems in the management of patients with epilepsy [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.2 ) ] . Nonetheless, any changes in dosage administration, or the addition or discontinuance of concomitant drugs should ordinarily be accompanied by close monitoring of clinical status and valproate plasma concentrations. Chemically it is designated as sodium hydrogen bis(2-propylpentanoate). Divalproex sodium has the following structure: Divalproex sodium occurs as a white powder with a characteristic odor. Depakote tablets are for oral administration. Depakote tablets are supplied in three dosage strengths containing divalproex sodium equivalent to 125 mg, 250 mg, or 500 mg of valproic acid. Inactive Ingredients Depakote tablets: cellulosic polymers, diacetylated monoglycerides, povidone, pregelatinized starch (contains corn starch), silica gel, talc, titanium dioxide, and vanillin. In addition, individual tablets contain: 125 mg tablets: FD&C Blue No. 1 and FD&C Red No. 40. 250 mg tablets: FD&C Yellow No. 6 and iron oxide. 500 mg tablets: D&C Red No. 30, FD&C Blue No. 2, and iron oxide. The following structure Divalproex sodium is a stable co-ordination compound comprised of sodium valproate and valproic acid in a 1:1 molar relationship and formed during the partial neutralization of valproic acid with 0.5 equivalent of sodium hydroxide. evidence.L:dosage_and_administration: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION Depakote tablets are intended for oral administration. Depakote tablets should be swallowed whole and should not be crushed or chewed. Patients should be informed to take Depakote every day as prescribed. If a dose is missed it should be taken as soon as possible, unless it is almost time for the next dose. If a dose is skipped, the patient should not double the next dose. Depakote is administered orally in divided doses. Depakote should be swallowed whole and should not be crushed or chewed ( 2.1 , 2.2 ). Mania: Initial dose is 750 mg daily, increasing as rapidly as possible to achieve therapeutic response or desired plasma level ( 2.1 ). The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day ( 2.1 , 2.2 ). Complex Partial Seizures: Start at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day to achieve optimal clinical response; if response is not satisfactory, check valproate plasma level; see full prescribing information for conversion to monotherapy ( 2.2 ). The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day ( 2.1 , 2.2 ). Absence Seizures: Start at 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day until seizure control or limiting side effects ( 2.2 ). The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day ( 2.1 , 2.2 ). The recommended initial dose is 750 mg daily in divided doses. The dose should be increased as rapidly as possible to achieve the lowest therapeutic dose which produces the desired clinical effect or the desired range of plasma concentrations. In placebo-controlled clinical trials of acute mania, patients were dosed to a clinical response with a trough plasma concentration between 50 and 125 mcg/mL. Maximum concentrations were generally achieved within 14 days. The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day. There is no body of evidence available from controlled trials to guide a clinician in the longer term management of a patient who improves during Depakote treatment of an acute manic episode. While it is generally agreed that pharmacological treatment beyond an acute response in mania is desirable, both for maintenance of the initial response and for prevention of new manic episodes, there are no data to support the benefits of Depakote in such longer-term treatment. Although there are no efficacy data that specifically address longer-term antimanic treatment with Depakote, the safety of Depakote in long-term use is supported by data from record reviews involving approximately 360 patients treated with Depakote for greater than 3 months. 2.2 Epilepsy Depakote tablets are administered orally. Depakote is indicated as monotherapy and adjunctive therapy in complex partial seizures in adults and pediatric patients down to the age of 10 years, and in simple and complex absence seizures. evidence.L:mechanism_of_action: 12.1 Mechanism of Action Divalproex sodium dissociates to the valproate ion in the gastrointestinal tract. The mechanisms by which valproate exerts its therapeutic effects have not been established. It has been suggested that its activity in epilepsy is related to increased brain concentrations of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA).
evidence.L:pharmacokinetics: 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption/Bioavailability Equivalent oral doses of Depakote (divalproex sodium) products and valproic acid capsules deliver equivalent quantities of valproate ion systemically. Although the rate of valproate ion absorption may vary with the formulation administered (liquid, solid, or sprinkle), conditions of use (e.g., fasting or postprandial) and the method of administration (e.g., whether the contents of the capsule are sprinkled on food or the capsule is taken intact), these differences should be of minor clinical importance under the steady state conditions achieved in chronic use in the treatment of epilepsy. However, it is possible that differences among the various valproate products in T max and C max could be important upon initiation of treatment. For example, in single dose studies, the effect of feeding had a greater influence on the rate of absorption of the tablet (increase in T max from 4 to 8 hours) than on the absorption of the sprinkle capsules (increase in T max from 3.3 to 4.8 hours). While the absorption rate from the G.I. tract and fluctuation in valproate plasma concentrations vary with dosing regimen and formulation, the efficacy of valproate as an anticonvulsant in chronic use is unlikely to be affected. Experience employing dosing regimens from once-a-day to four-times-a-day, as well as studies in primate epilepsy models involving constant rate infusion, indicate that total daily systemic bioavailability (extent of absorption) is the primary determinant of seizure control and that differences in the ratios of plasma peak to trough concentrations between valproate formulations are inconsequential from a practical clinical standpoint. Whether or not rate of absorption influences the efficacy of valproate as an antimanic or antimigraine agent is unknown. Co-administration of oral valproate products with food and substitution among the various Depakote and valproic acid formulations should cause no clinical problems in the management of patients with epilepsy [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.2 ) ] . Nonetheless, any changes in dosage administration, or the addition or discontinuance of concomitant drugs should ordinarily be accompanied by close monitoring of clinical status and valproate plasma concentrations. Distribution Protein Binding The plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent and the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Protein binding of valproate is reduced in the elderly, in patients with chronic hepatic diseases, in patients with renal impairment, and in the presence of other drugs (e.g., aspirin). Conversely, valproate may displace certain protein-bound drugs (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine, warfarin, and tolbutamide) [see Drug Interactions ( 7.2 ) for more detailed information on the pharmacokinetic interactions of valproate with other drugs ] . CNS Distribution Valproate concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) approximate unbound concentrations in plasma (about 10% of total concentration). Metabolism Valproate is metabolized almost entirely by the liver. In adult patients on monotherapy, 30-50% of an administered dose appears in urine as a glucuronide conjugate. Mitochondrial β-oxidation is the other major metabolic pathway, typically accounting for over 40% of the dose. Usually, less than 15-20% of the dose is eliminated by other oxidative mechanisms. Less than 3% of an administered dose is excreted unchanged in urine. The relationship between dose and total valproate concentration is nonlinear; concentration does not increase proportionally with the dose, but rather, increases to a lesser extent due to saturable plasma protein binding. The kinetics of unbound drug are linear. Elimination Mean plasma clearance and volume of distribution for total valproate are 0.56 L/hr/1.73 m 2 and 11 L/1.73 m 2 , respectively. Mean plasma clearance and volume of distribution for free valproate are 4.6 L/hr/1.

evidence.L:warnings_and_cautions: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Birth defects, decreased IQ, and neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure: Should not be used to treat women with epilepsy or bipolar disorder who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant or to treat a woman of childbearing potential unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable ( 5.2 , 5.3 , 5.4 ) Pancreatitis: Depakote should ordinarily be discontinued ( 5.5 ) Suicidal behavior or ideation: Antiepileptic drugs, including Depakote, increase the risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior ( 5.7 ) Bleeding and other hematopoietic disorders: Monitor platelet counts and coagulation tests ( 5.8 ) Hyperammonemia and hyperammonemic encephalopathy: Measure ammonia level if unexplained lethargy and vomiting or changes in mental status, and also with concomitant topiramate use; consider discontinuation of valproate therapy ( 5.6 , 5.9 , 5.10 ) Hypothermia: Hypothermia has been reported during valproate therapy with occur in patients using concomitant topiramate ( 5.11 ) Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)/Multiorgan Hypersensitivity Reactions, serious dermatologic reactions, and angioedema: Discontinue Depakote unless an alternate etiology is established ( 4 , 5.12 , 5.13 , 5.14 ) 5.1 Hepatotoxicity General Information on Hepatotoxicity Hepatic failure resulting in fatalities has occurred in patients receiving valproate. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment. Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months of valproate therapy. However, healthcare providers should not rely totally on serum biochemistry since these tests may not be abnormal in all instances, but should also consider the results of careful interim medical history and physical examination. Caution should be observed when administering valproate products to patients with a prior history of hepatic disease. Patients on multiple anticonvulsants, children, those with congenital metabolic disorders, those with severe seizure disorders accompanied by mental retardation, and those with organic brain disease may be at particular risk. See below, “Patients with Known or Suspected Mitochondrial Disease.” Experience has indicated that children under the age of two years are at a considerably increased risk of developing fatal hepatotoxicity, especially those with the aforementioned conditions. When Depakote is used in this patient group, it should be used with extreme caution and as a sole agent. The benefits of therapy should be weighed against the risks. In progressively older patient groups experience in epilepsy has indicated that the incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases considerably. Patients with Known or Suspected Mitochondrial Disease Depakote is contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder [see Contraindications ( 4 ) ] . why.claim: Sugary drinks like fruit juice pull water into the gut. They can raise stoma output, so guidelines say to limit them.
Drinks with a lot of simple sugar draw water into the bowel. They are usually limited in short bowel syndrome.
With an end-jejunostomy, an oral rehydration solution is the preferred drink to replace lost fluid and salt.

why.claim: With an end-jejunostomy, plain water and other low-salt drinks can pull salt (sodium) into the gut and raise output. So these drinks are usually limited, and an oral rehydration solution is used instead.
An oral rehydration solution with glucose and salt is the preferred drink to replace lost fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.

final.verdict: If an energy drink like Red Bull is sugary and has caffeine, the guidelines say both of those are usually limited because they can raise stoma output and fluid loss.

why.claim: Sugary drinks with a high concentration, like fruit juice and regular soda, pull water into the gut. They can raise stoma output. Guidelines say to limit them whatever your anatomy.
Concentrated simple sugars, including sweetened drinks, draw water into the bowel and are usually limited in short bowel syndrome.
Caffeine can increase output and fluid loss and is usually limited in short bowel syndrome.
People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium.
Thirst, dark or reduced urine, dizziness when you stand up, and rising stoma output are warning signs of dehydration. Tell your care team promptly if you notice them.
An oral rehydration solution (ORS), which contains both glucose and salts, is the preferred drink for replacing fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome.
For short bowel syndrome, ORS with about 90 to 120 mmol/L sodium is generally recommended. That is more sodium than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.

draft.verdict: The guidelines name oral rehydration solution as the preferred drink to replace fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome, and I found nothing in the sources I checked against it for your body, but the type you use matters because some formulas have less salt than short bowel guidelines suggest.

why.claim: A glucose-and-salt oral rehydration solution is the preferred drink to replace fluid and salt losses in short bowel syndrome.
It works because sugar (glucose) and salt (sodium) are taken in together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them. You still have 100 to 200 cm of small bowel.
People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of losing too much fluid and having low sodium.
For short bowel syndrome, rehydration drinks with about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium are usually recommended. That is more salt than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
The WHO reduced-osmolarity formula has 75 mmol/L of sodium. It was designed for sudden diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.
Sugary drinks like fruit juice and regular soda pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output, so they are not the same as an oral rehydration solution.
Among people with an ileostomy who logged it, 7 said it helped, 1 said no change, and 6 said it made things worse. That is a mixed picture, and these are self-reports, not a study.

why.claim: Most people whose colon is still connected handle ordinary watery drinks, like water, better than people with no colon. That's because the colon takes up water and salt.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there. But the type of stoma alone doesn't guarantee how your gut handles things.

why.claim: People with short bowel syndrome whose colon is still connected usually handle plain water better than people without a colon. That's because the colon takes up water and salt.
Advice to limit plain water is mainly for people with an end-jejunostomy (no colon). In their bodies, water can pull salt into the gut and raise output.
Your stoma type alone doesn't show exactly how much small bowel you have left. So the general rule isn't a guarantee for any one person.
Tell your care team quickly if you notice thirst, dark urine or less of it, dizziness when you stand up, or more output than usual. These are warning signs of dehydration.

why.claim: WHO ORS works because sugar (glucose) and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them. You have over 200 cm of small bowel, which is where this happens.

WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L. It was made for sudden diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.
For short bowel syndrome, ORS with sodium of about 90 to 120 mmol/L is generally recommended.
Most people whose colon is still connected handle plain fluids like water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there. But the type of stoma alone doesn't tell you how much small bowel is left, so your exact anatomy matters.
Among people with a colostomy who logged ORS, 3 said it helped, 4 noticed no difference and 5 said it hurt. Some of these logs are synthetic.

draft.verdict: I found nothing in the sources I checked that speaks against oral rehydration solution for a body like yours, though people with a colostomy have reported mixed results with it.

why.claim: Oral rehydration solution works because sugar and salt are taken up together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them. You have over 200 cm of small bowel, which is where this happens.
This kind of drink is the preferred way to replace lost fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome. It matters most for people with a jejunostomy.
People whose colon is still connected usually handle plain water better than people with a jejunostomy, because the colon soaks up water and salt.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there. But the type of stoma alone doesn't tell you how much small bowel is left.
Salt level matters. For short bowel syndrome, about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium is generally recommended. Many store-bought rehydration drinks have less.
The WHO formula has 75 mmol/L of sodium. It was designed for sudden diarrhea and has less salt than the range usually given for short bowel syndrome.
Watch for signs of dehydration: thirst, dark urine or less urine, feeling dizzy when you stand up, and more stoma output. Tell your care team quickly if you notice any of these.
Among people with a colostomy who logged this drink, 3 said it helped, 4 noticed no change and 5 said it made things worse. These are self-reports, not a study.

G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon.text: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.

G:pd-2017#ors-sodium.text: For short bowel syndrome, oral rehydration solutions with a sodium concentration of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are generally recommended; this is higher than many commercial rehydration drinks.

G:who-ors#purpose.text: Oral rehydration solution works because glucose and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel, carrying water with them.

G:who-ors#reduced-osmolarity-composition.text: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (2003) contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L (total 245 mOsm/L). It was designed for acute diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.

why.claim: For short bowel syndrome, the guidelines prefer a rehydration drink made with sugar (glucose) and salts to replace lost fluid and salt.
These drinks work because sugar and salt are taken up together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them.
For short bowel, the usual advice is a rehydration drink with about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium (salt). That is more salt than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
The standard WHO formula has 75 mmol/L of sodium. It was made for sudden diarrhea, and its salt is below the range usually used for short bowel.
Because your colon is still connected, it soaks up water and salt. So people like you usually handle plain drinks like water better than people with an end-jejunostomy.
8 of 12 people with your type of anatomy (small bowel joined to colon) logged that a rehydration drink helped. 2 said it hurt and 2 noticed no change.

draft.verdict: Peanut butter is mostly fat, and the guidelines say that with your colon still connected, limiting fat is often useful, so it's worth asking your team how it fits for you.

why.claim: Cutting back on fat is mainly useful when the colon is still connected, because of oxalate and fatty-acid effects in the colon.
With the colon connected, poor fat absorption raises oxalate absorption and the risk of kidney stones. Many teams advise this group to limit high-oxalate foods.
Diet advice is different for each anatomy group, so advice meant for people with no colon may not apply to you.
Of 11 people with your anatomy who logged peanut butter, 7 said it helped, 3 noticed no change, and 1 said it hurt. These are self-reports, not a trial.

draft.verdict: Potassium chloride ER is an extended-release tablet, and the guidelines flag this type of tablet for people with an ostomy and no working colon, so it's worth checking with your pharmacist.

why.claim: This product is an extended-release tablet.
The label says to swallow the tablets whole, without crushing, chewing or sucking.
The label says the potassium chloride in these tablets is fully absorbed before it leaves the small intestine. You have over 200 cm of small bowel, which works in your favor.
How well medicines are absorbed depends more on how much healthy small bowel is left than on the type of stoma.
Time-release tablets need enough time in the small bowel to let out their medicine. If the bowel is shorter or moves things through fast, part of a dose can leave the body before it is released.
Slow-release products may let out part of their dose in the colon. Without a colon, they have less time and less surface to do that.
A study of ostomy patients put extended-release products in the highest-risk group for not dissolving. Solutions were in the lowest-risk group.
Of 13 people with an ileostomy who logged this medicine, 2 said it helped, 5 noticed no change, and 6 said it caused problems.

why.claim: This is a plain tablet that releases the medicine right away. It has no timed-release design.
The label describes the tablets as immediate-release and uncoated.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel. Many plain, immediate-release medicines can still be absorbed when that part is still there.

How well pills are absorbed depends mostly on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is. Your length is unknown, so this can't be judged for sure.
In studies of people who had part of their bowel removed, many medicines were absorbed less well. The effect differed from one medicine to the next.
The label says it can be taken with meals, but blood levels are a little higher when it's taken on an empty stomach.
A liquid form of this medicine is also sold. Liquids may absorb more reliably in short bowel, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.

why.claim: Coreg CR is an extended-release capsule.
The label says the capsule and what is inside it should not be crushed, chewed, or taken in divided doses.

draft.verdict: There's nothing in the sources I checked that warns against this cefdinir capsule for your anatomy, but how well it absorbs depends on how much small bowel you have, and nobody knows that length yet.

why.claim: This cefdinir is a plain capsule, not a timed-release or coated one. Its listed inactive ingredient is carboxymethylcellulose calcium. That ingredient is not a sugar alcohol, which is the kind of ingredient that can increase output.
The product is a capsule.
Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel. So many plain immediate-release medicines can still be absorbed when that part of the bowel remains.
How well medicines are absorbed depends mostly on the length and health of the small bowel you still have. Your length is not known.
Even in people with a full bowel, only about 16% to 21% of a cefdinir capsule dose gets absorbed into the body.
A review found that 29 of 37 medicines were absorbed less after part of the bowel was removed. The effect was different for each medicine, so nobody can predict it for one person.

Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel, so many plain tablets (not slow-release) can still be absorbed when that part remains.
How well medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#antimotility: Antimotility medicines (for example loperamide) are a mainstay to slow transit and reduce output; timing relative to meals is set by the care team.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#diet-simple-sugars: Concentrated simple sugars (sweets, syrups, sweetened drinks) draw water into the bowel and are generally limited in short bowel syndrome.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.
evidence.G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.
evidence.G:pd-2017#lactose: Lactose does not need to be removed for most people with short bowel syndrome; small portions of dairy, especially cheese and yogurt, are often tolerated.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#sugar-alcohols: Sorbitol, xylitol, mannitol and other sugar alcohols are poorly absorbed, draw water into the gut, and can raise stoma output or diarrhea; they are common inactive ingredients in liquid medicines and sugar-free products.
evidence.G:pg139#time-release: Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.

draft.ask: ASK: मेरी इलियोस्टॉमी के लिए, क्या मैं जो ORS पीता/पीती हूँ उसमें सोडियम शॉर्ट बाउल के लिए सुझाए गए लगभग 90 से 120 mmol/L जितना है?

careTeamAnswers.summary: एक दूसरे उपयोगकर्ता ने बताया कि उनकी अपनी केयर टीम के डॉक्टर ने कहा कि WHO वाला फॉर्मूला अचानक दस्त के लिए बना था और उन्हें ज़्यादा नमक चाहिए।

एक दूसरे उपयोगकर्ता ने बताया कि उनकी अपनी केयर टीम की डायटीशियन ने कहा कि दुकान पर मिलने वाले कई ORS में शॉर्ट बाउल के लिए इस्तेमाल होने वाले ORS से कम सोडियम होता है, और उन्होंने एक नुस्खा दिया जिसे उन्होंने मंज़ूर किया था।
एक दूसरे उपयोगकर्ता ने बताया कि उनकी अपनी केयर टीम की डायटीशियन ने कहा कि थोड़ा नींबू या बिना चीनी वाला फ्लेवर आम तौर पर ठीक है, पर सॉर्बिटॉल वाले फ्लेवर से बचें।

draft.verdict: दिशानिर्देशों में ओरल रिहाइड्रेशन सॉल्यूशन (ORS) को शॉर्ट बाउल में पानी और नमक की कमी पूरी करने के लिए सबसे अच्छा पेय बताया गया है। पर एक बात ध्यान देने की है: दुकान पर मिलने वाले कई ORS में नमक (सोडियम) उतना नहीं होता जितना शॉर्ट बाउल के लिए आम तौर पर सुझाया जाता है।

why.claim: शॉर्ट बाउल में पानी और नमक की कमी पूरी करने के लिए ग्लूकोज़ और नमक वाला ORS सबसे अच्छा पेय माना जाता है।
ORS इसलिए काम करता है क्योंकि छोटी आंत में ग्लूकोज़ और सोडियम साथ-साथ सोखे जाते हैं और अपने साथ पानी भी अंदर ले जाते हैं।
शॉर्ट बाउल के लिए आम तौर पर लगभग 90 से 120 mmol/L सोडियम वाला ORS सुझाया जाता है। यह दुकान पर मिलने वाले कई रिहाइड्रेशन पेयों से ज़्यादा है।
WHO का कम-ऑस्मोलैरिटी वाला ORS (सोडियम 75, क्लोराइड 65, ग्लूकोज़ 75, पोटैशियम 20, साइट्रेट 10 mmol/L) अचानक दस्त के लिए बनाया गया था। इसका सोडियम शॉर्ट बाउल के लिए बताए गए स्तर से कम है।
इलियोस्टॉमी वाले लोगों में पानी की कमी और सोडियम कम होने का खतरा ज़्यादा होता है।
जूस और मीठे सोडा जैसे बहुत मीठे पेय आंत में पानी खींचते हैं और स्टोमा से निकलने वाली मात्रा बढ़ा सकते हैं।
इलियोस्टॉमी वाले लोगों के अनुभव मिले-जुले हैं: 14 में से 7 ने कहा फायदा हुआ, 6 ने कहा नुकसान हुआ और 1 ने कहा कोई फर्क नहीं पड़ा।
एक दूसरे उपयोगकर्ता ने बताया कि उनकी अपनी केयर टीम के डॉक्टर ने कहा कि WHO वाला फॉर्मूला अचानक दस्त के लिए बना था और उन्हें ज़्यादा नमक चाहिए।

draft.verdict: سوليفيناسين سكسينات قرص عادي (فوري المفعول)، ومثل هذه الأقراص يمكن أن تُمتص غالبًا في الجزء العلوي من الأمعاء، لكن مع بقاء أقل من 100 سم من الأمعاء الدقيقة قد يقلّ الامتصاص، وهذا يستحق السؤال عنه.

why.claim: الدواء المسجَّل هو قرص (TABLET).
معظم الأدوية التي تؤخذ بالفم تُمتص في الجزء العلوي من الأمعاء الدقيقة (أول الصائم)، لذلك كثير من الأقراص العادية فورية المفعول يمكن أن تُمتص إذا بقي هذا الجزء.
الأقراص العادية سريعة الذوبان تُعدّ من الأشكال قليلة الخطورة من ناحية الذوبان عند من لديهم فغرة.
مدى امتصاص الأدوية يرتبط بطول الأمعاء الدقيقة المتبقية وصحتها أكثر من نوع الفغرة. وأنت لديك أقل من 100 سم، لذلك قد يكون الامتصاص أقل.
هذا الدواء يحتوي على اللاكتوز كمادة غير فعالة. لكن معظم مرضى متلازمة الأمعاء القصيرة لا يحتاجون إلى تجنب اللاكتوز تمامًا.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#anatomy-groups: Short bowel syndrome is described in three anatomy groups: end-jejunostomy (no colon), jejuno-colic (small bowel joined to part of the colon), and jejuno-ileo-colic (some ileum kept, joined to the colon). Advice on fluids and diet differs between these groups.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#antimotility: Antimotility medicines (for example loperamide) are a mainstay to slow transit and reduce output; timing relative to meals is set by the care team.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#diet-simple-sugars: Concentrated simple sugars (sweets, syrups, sweetened drinks) draw water into the bowel and are generally limited in short bowel syndrome.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.
evidence.G:pd-2017#lactose: Lactose does not need to be removed for most people with short bowel syndrome; small portions of dairy, especially cheese and yogurt, are often tolerated.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#sugar-alcohols: Sorbitol, xylitol, mannitol and other sugar alcohols are poorly absorbed, draw water into the gut, and can raise stoma output or diarrhea; they are common inactive ingredients in liquid medicines and sugar-free products.
evidence.G:remane-2025#formulation-classes: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).
evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

why.claim: Um soro de reidratação oral com glicose e sais é a bebida preferida para repor líquido e sal no intestino curto.
O soro funciona porque a glicose e o sódio são absorvidos juntos no intestino delgado e levam a água junto.

A SRO da OMS de osmolaridade reduzida tem sódio 75 mmol/L, cloreto 65, glicose 75, potássio 20 e citrato 10 mmol/L. Foi feita para diarreia aguda, e o sódio dela fica abaixo da faixa usada no intestino curto.
Para intestino curto, costuma-se recomendar soro com sódio de cerca de 90 a 120 mmol/L, mais alto que muitos soros comerciais.
Quem tem o cólon ligado ao intestino costuma tolerar melhor líquidos comuns, como água, do que quem tem jejunostomia, porque o cólon absorve água e sódio.
Entre pessoas com intestino delgado ligado ao cólon, 8 de 12 disseram que o soro ajudou, 2 que foi neutro e 2 que piorou.

sourcesChecked: Registros de la comunidad por anatomía

swapToAskAbout.text: Si está perdiendo mucho líquido o sal, puede preguntar si una solución de rehidratación oral le conviene además del agua.

draft.verdict: No encontré nada en las fuentes que revisé que vaya en contra del agua cuando el colon sigue conectado. Las guías dicen que con el colon conectado el agua suele tolerarse mejor.

why.claim: La mayoría de las personas con intestino corto y el colon conectado toleran mejor el agua que quienes tienen una yeyunostomía, porque el colon absorbe agua y sal.
Las guías describen tres grupos según la anatomía, y los consejos sobre líquidos cambian entre ellos. Su grupo es intestino delgado unido al colon.
El consejo de limitar el agua sola es para personas con yeyunostomía terminal (sin colon), porque en ellas puede sacar sal y subir la salida.
En el intestino corto, la solución de rehidratación oral (SRO) es la bebida preferida para reponer líquido y sal, sobre todo con yeyunostomía.
Para el intestino corto se suele recomendar una SRO con unos 90 a 120 mmol/L de sodio. Es más que muchas bebidas de rehidratación que se venden.
Las bebidas dulces, como el jugo o los refrescos normales, pueden subir la diarrea. Las guías aconsejan limitarlas en cualquier anatomía.
Entre las personas con el intestino delgado unido al colon que registraron el agua, 5 de 13 dijeron que les ayudó, 8 no notaron cambio y a ninguna le hizo daño.
Otro usuario con el colon conectado contó lo que le dijo su propia dietista: quienes tienen colon suelen tolerar mejor el agua, y su plan de líquidos se hizo a su medida.

G:aga-sbs#anatomy-groups.text: Short bowel syndrome is described in three anatomy groups: end-jejunostomy (no colon), jejuno-colic (small bowel joined to part of the colon), and jejuno-ileo-colic (some ileum kept, joined to the colon). Advice on fluids and diet differs between these groups.

G:aga-sbs#fluids-hypertonic.text: Hypertonic, sugary drinks such as fruit juice and regular soda pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output or diarrhea in short bowel syndrome; they are best limited regardless of anatomy.

G:aga-sbs#fluids-ors.text: A glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink to replace fluid and sodium losses in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.

G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon.text: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.

G:pd-2017#ors-sodium.text: For short bowel syndrome, oral rehydration solutions with a sodium concentration of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are generally recommended; this is higher than many commercial rehydration drinks.

final.verdict: No encontré nada en las fuentes que revisé que vaya en contra del agua cuando el colon sigue conectado. Las guías dicen que con el colon conectado el agua suele tolerarse mejor.

why.claim: La mayoría de las personas con intestino corto y el colon conectado toleran mejor el agua que quienes tienen una yeyunostomía, porque el colon absorbe agua y sal.
Las guías describen tres grupos según la anatomía, y los consejos sobre líquidos cambian entre ellos.
En el intestino corto, la solución de rehidratación oral (SRO) es la bebida preferida para reponer líquido y sal, sobre todo con yeyunostomía.
Para el intestino corto se suele recomendar una SRO con unos 90 a 120 mmol/L de sodio. Es más que muchas bebidas de rehidratación que se venden.
Las bebidas dulces, como el jugo o los refrescos normales, pueden subir la diarrea. Las guías aconsejan limitarlas en cualquier anatomía.
Entre las personas con el intestino delgado unido al colon que registraron el agua, 5 de 13 dijeron que les ayudó, 8 no notaron cambio y a ninguna le hizo daño.
Otro usuario contó lo que le dijo su propia dietista: quienes tienen colon suelen tolerar mejor el agua, y su plan de líquidos se hizo a su medida. No es un consejo de su propio equipo de salud.

draft.ask: ASK: 我是回肠造口，剩下超过200厘米小肠，结肠没接通。Bactrim 片剂在我身上能正常吸收吗？

diagram.label: Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel

sourcesChecked: Guidelines: antibiotics diarrhea high output stoma dehydration
draft.verdict: Bactrim 是普通片剂。按指南，这类药大多在小肠上段吸收。我查过的资料里没有找到针对您情况的问题，但标签里讲药物怎么吸收的那部分缺失，所以不能确定。

why.claim: 这个药是片剂（TABLET）。
标签列出的辅料是：多库酯钠、苯甲酸钠、羧甲淀粉钠、硬脂酸镁。里面没有列出山梨醇这类糖醇。
大多数口服药在小肠上段（空肠的前段）吸收。只要这一段还在，很多普通即释药仍然能吸收。
药物吸收得好不好，主要看剩下的小肠有多长、有多健康，而不太看是哪种造口。
在造口人群中，普通的快速溶解片剂属于“溶解风险不高”的一类。风险高的是缓释片和肠溶片。
结肠主要对缓释药有影响，因为缓释药可能有一部分在结肠里释放。普通片剂不属于这类。
回肠造口的人更容易脱水和缺钠。
如果口渴、尿少或颜色深、站起来头晕，或者造口排出量变多，这些是脱水的警示信号，要尽快告诉医护人员。

G:aga-sbs#dehydration-signs.text: Thirst, dark or reduced urine, dizziness on standing, and rising stoma output are warning signs of dehydration that should be raised with the care team promptly.

G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio.text: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.

G:remane-2025#formulation-classes.text: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).

G:sood-2013#colon-slow-release.text: The large intestine matters mainly for slow-release products, which may release part of their dose there; without a colon, those products have less time and surface to release.

G:sood-2013#ileostomy-dehydration.text: People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium, and medicines such as diuretics and laxatives can add to that risk.

G:sood-2013#residual-length.text: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

L:description.text: Inactive ingredients: Docusate sodium 85%, sodium benzoate 15%, sodium starch glycolate, magnesium stearate

ORS పని చేసే విధానం: చిన్న ప్రేగులో గ్లూకోజ్, సోడియం కలిసి శోషించబడతాయి, వాటితో పాటు నీటిని కూడా లోపలికి తీసుకెళ్తాయి.
షార్ట్ బవెల్‌కు సాధారణంగా లీటరుకు సుమారు 90 నుండి 120 mmol సోడియం ఉన్న ORS సూచిస్తారు. ఇది చాలా వాణిజ్య రీహైడ్రేషన్ పానీయాల కంటే ఎక్కువ.
WHO తక్కువ-ఆస్మోలారిటీ ORS లో సోడియం 75 mmol/L ఉంటుంది. ఇది అకస్మాత్తుగా వచ్చే విరేచనాల కోసం రూపొందించబడింది. దీని సోడియం షార్ట్ బవెల్‌కు సూచించే స్థాయి కంటే తక్కువ.
పెద్ద ప్రేగు (కోలన్) కలిసి ఉన్నవారు నీటిని సాధారణంగా ఎక్కువగా తట్టుకుంటారు, ఎందుకంటే కోలన్ నీటిని, సోడియంను శోషిస్తుంది.
మీలాంటి శరీర నిర్మాణం (చిన్న ప్రేగు కోలన్‌కు కలిసి ఉన్న) ఉన్న 12 మందిలో 8 మంది ORS సహాయపడిందని, 2 మంది ఇబ్బంది పెట్టిందని, 2 మంది తేడా లేదని నమోదు చేశారు.

careTeamAnswers.summary: మరో వినియోగదారు తన సొంత డైటీషియన్ చెప్పినట్లు నివేదించారు: షాపుల్లో దొరికే చాలా ORS లలో షార్ట్ బవెల్‌కు వాడే దానికంటే సోడియం తక్కువ ఉంటుంది; ఆమె ఆమోదించిన ఒక రెసిపీ ఇచ్చారు.
మరో వినియోగదారు తన సొంత డైటీషియన్ చెప్పినట్లు నివేదించారు: కొద్దిగా నిమ్మరసం లేదా చక్కెర లేని ఫ్లేవర్ సాధారణంగా పర్వాలేదు, కానీ సార్బిటాల్ ఉన్న ఫ్లేవర్లను నివారించాలి.
మరో వినియోగదారు తన సొంత డాక్టర్ చెప్పినట్లు నివేదించారు: WHO ఫార్ములా అకస్మాత్తు విరేచనాల కోసం రూపొందించబడింది, తనకు ఇంకా ఎక్కువ ఉప్పు అవసరం.

diagram.label: A colon absorbs much of the water and salt

G:aga-sbs#fluids-ors.text: A glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink to replace fluid and sodium losses in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.

G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon.text: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.

G:pd-2017#ors-sodium.text: For short bowel syndrome, oral rehydration solutions with a sodium concentration of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are generally recommended; this is higher than many commercial rehydration drinks.

G:who-ors#purpose.text: Oral rehydration solution works because glucose and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel, carrying water with them.

G:who-ors#reduced-osmolarity-composition.text: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (2003) contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L (total 245 mOsm/L). It was designed for acute diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.

draft.verdict: Trong các nguồn tôi đã kiểm tra, không có điều gì nói riêng về nước dừa cho người có hậu môn nhân tạo hồi tràng như bạn, nhưng người có hậu môn nhân tạo hồi tràng dễ bị mất nước và thiếu muối hơn.

why.claim: Người có hậu môn nhân tạo hồi tràng dễ bị mất nước và thiếu muối (natri) hơn người khác.
Đồ uống ưu trương, nhiều đường như nước ép trái cây và nước ngọt có ga kéo nước vào ruột và có thể làm tăng lượng dịch ra túi. Nên hạn chế loại này.
Dung dịch bù nước điện giải (ORS) có đường và muối là đồ uống được ưu tiên để bù nước và muối bị mất trong hội chứng ruột ngắn.
Với hội chứng ruột ngắn, ORS thường được khuyên có natri khoảng 90 đến 120 mmol/L. Mức này cao hơn nhiều loại nước bù điện giải bán sẵn.
Khát nước, nước tiểu sẫm màu hoặc ít đi, chóng mặt khi đứng dậy, và lượng dịch ra túi tăng lên là dấu hiệu mất nước. Hãy báo sớm cho đội chăm sóc.
Chưa có người dùng nào ghi lại trải nghiệm với nước dừa, kể cả người có hậu môn nhân tạo hồi tràng.

draft.verdict: Il y a peu d'éléments nouveaux : la notice dit que la prise avec un repas ne change pas la quantité absorbée, mais elle ne dit pas où le médicament est absorbé dans l'intestin. La forme à libération prolongée reste le point à voir avec votre pharmacien.

why.claim: Ce produit est un comprimé à libération prolongée.
La notice dit qu'après un repas très gras, la quantité de la forme active du médicament (appelée MHD) dans le sang est la même qu'à jeun. Les repas ne semblent donc pas changer l'absorption.
Les parties de la notice que j'ai lues ne disent pas à quel endroit de l'intestin le médicament est absorbé. Elles n'ont pas été testées chez des personnes avec un intestin raccourci.
La plupart des médicaments sont absorbés dans le haut de l'intestin grêle. Beaucoup de médicaments à libération immédiate restent donc absorbés si cette partie est encore là.
Les formes à libération prolongée ont besoin d'un long passage normal dans l'intestin pour libérer le médicament. On les évite en général après une grande résection de l'intestin grêle.
Si l'intestin est plus court ou le transit plus rapide, une partie de la dose peut sortir du corps avant d'être libérée.
L'absorption dépend surtout de la longueur et de l'état de l'intestin grêle restant. Ici, cette longueur n'est pas connue.

Une revue d'études a montré une baisse de l'absorption pour 29 médicaments sur 37 après une résection de l'intestin. Cet effet dépend de chaque médicament et ne permet pas de prévoir ce qui se passera pour une personne précise.
La notice dit d'avaler le comprimé entier, sans le couper, l'écraser ni le croquer. Toute décision sur la façon de le prendre revient à votre pharmacien ou à votre prescripteur.
Les formes liquides peuvent être mieux absorbées. Mais elles contiennent souvent des sucres-alcools, qui peuvent augmenter les selles.

G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio.text: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.

G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms.text: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.

G:hong-2021#absorption-findings.text: Across studies reviewed, absorption was decreased for 29 of 37 drugs after intestinal resection, and 6 drugs lost clinical effect; the effect was drug-specific, so it cannot be turned into a single probability for one person.

G:pg139#extended-release-avoid.text: Extended-release products are generally avoided after extensive resection; an immediate-release or liquid version of the same drug is often a question worth asking the pharmacist about.

G:pg139#liquid-forms.text: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.

G:pg139#time-release.text: Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.

G:sood-2013#residual-length.text: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

L:dosage_and_administration.text: Swallow oxcarbazepine extended-release tablets whole.

L:pharmacokinetics.text: Single dose administration of 600 mg oxcarbazepine extended-release tablets following a high fat meal (800 –1000 calories) produced MHD exposure (AUC) equivalent to that produced under fasting conditions.

draft.ask: ASK: Sa maikli kong maliit na bituka, paano natin malalaman kung gumagana nang maayos ang rosuvastatin sa akin?

diagram.label: Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel

sourcesChecked: Guidelines: immediate-release absorption, release forms, malabsorption, monitoring, drug-specific absorption
draft.verdict: Wala akong nakitang tiyak na problema sa rosuvastatin sa mga pinagkunang sinuri ko, pero walang makapagsasabi nang sigurado kung gaano ito nasisipsip sa maikli mong maliit na bituka, kaya sulit itong itanong sa parmasyutiko.

why.claim: Ito ay tabletang may film coating. Agad itong naglalabas ng gamot. Hindi ito pinahaba o inantala ang paglabas.

Karamihan ng iniinom na gamot ay nasisipsip sa itaas na bahagi ng maliit na bituka. Kaya maraming karaniwang tableta na agad naglalabas ng gamot ang nasisipsip pa rin kung may natira pang bahaging iyon.
Ang mga gamot na pinahaba o inantala ang paglabas (kasama ang enteric-coated) ang karaniwang iniiwasan pagkatapos ng malaking operasyon sa maliit na bituka. Hindi ganoong uri ang tabletang ito.
Ang pagsipsip ng gamot ay nakadepende sa haba at kalusugan ng natitirang maliit na bituka.

Sa isang malaking pagsusuri ng mga pag-aaral, bumaba ang pagsipsip ng 29 sa 37 gamot pagkatapos ng operasyon sa bituka. Iba-iba ito sa bawat gamot, kaya hindi ito masasabi nang eksakto para sa isang tao.
Dahil iba-iba ang epekto sa bawat gamot, dapat isa-isahin ang bawat gamot kasama ang doktor o parmasyutiko.
Sinasabi ng label na mga 20% lang ng gamot ang talagang napupunta sa dugo, kahit sa karaniwang tao.
Sinasabi ng label na lunukin nang buo ang tableta.
Kung parang hindi gumagana ang gamot gaya ng inaasahan, maaaring hindi ito nasisipsip nang maayos. Dapat itong sabihin sa doktor o parmasyutiko.
Kapag mahirap hulaan ang pagsipsip pagkatapos ng operasyon, puwedeng bantayan ng doktor nang mabuti ang epekto ng gamot.

G:aga-sbs#medications-monitoring.text: For drugs with a narrow therapeutic range, clinicians may check drug blood levels or watch the clinical effect closely, because absorption after resection is hard to predict.

G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio.text: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.

G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms.text: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.

G:hong-2021#absorption-findings.text: Across studies reviewed, absorption was decreased for 29 of 37 drugs after intestinal resection, and 6 drugs lost clinical effect; the effect was drug-specific, so it cannot be turned into a single probability for one person.

G:hong-2021#drug-specific.text: Because the change in absorption differs from drug to drug, each medicine should be considered individually with the prescriber or pharmacist.

G:sood-2013#residual-length.text: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

draft.ask: ASK: Dahil may end-jejunostomy ako, gaano kadalas dapat i-check ang sodium at hydration ko habang umiinom ng spironolactone suspension?
draft.verdict: Malamang na mas madaling ma-absorb ang likidong gamot na ito, pero ang spironolactone ay diuretic, at maaari itong dagdagan ang panganib ng dehydration at mababang sodium sa taong may stoma, kaya mainam itong pag-usapan sa inyong care team.

why.claim: Ang gamot na ito ay suspension, isang likidong anyo.
Sa short bowel syndrome, maaaring mas maaasahan ang pag-absorb ng likidong gamot kaysa sa solid na tableta, pero madalas may sugar alcohol ang likidong gamot na puwedeng magpalakas ng output.
Ang sorbitol at iba pang sugar alcohol ay humihila ng tubig papunta sa bituka at puwedeng magpataas ng stoma output.

Bahagi lang ng listahan ng inactive ingredients ang nakita ko: sorbic acid, potassium sorbate, citric acid anhydrous. why.claim: 含葡萄糖和电解质的口服补液盐，是短肠综合征补充水分和盐分的首选饮料。

结肠还连着的人，结肠能吸收水和盐，所以一般比没有结肠的人更能耐受白水这类普通饮料。
普通运动饮料钠少糖多，不能代替短肠综合征用的补液盐。

draft.verdict: Nada nas fontes que consultei aponta um problema de absorção do SINGULAIR (montelucaste) comprimido revestido com a sua ileostomia. Mas partes da bula estavam faltando, então isso não é uma garantia.

why.claim: O registro do produto diz que é um comprimido revestido.
Comprimidos simples, que se dissolvem rápido, estão no grupo de menor risco de não dissolver em quem tem estomia. Os de liberação prolongada e os com revestimento entérico são os de maior risco.
A maioria dos remédios é absorvida no começo do intestino delgado. Por isso, muitos comprimidos de liberação imediata ainda são absorvidos quando essa parte continua lá.
O quanto um remédio é absorvido depende mais do comprimento e da saúde do intestino delgado que sobrou do que do tipo de estomia.
O intestino grosso importa principalmente para remédios de liberação lenta, que soltam parte da dose lá.
Na bula, em média 64% da dose tomada pela boca chega ao sangue.

Os ingredientes inativos listados são celulose microcristalina, lactose mono-hidratada e croscarmelose sódica. Nenhum deles é sorbitol nem outro álcool de açúcar. A lactose está na lista; se você tem dúvida sobre lactose, vale perguntar.
Quem tem ileostomia tem mais risco de desidratação e sódio baixo. Isso é útil saber em geral, mas não é algo que encontrei sobre este remédio.

draft.verdict: बेनिकार (olmesartan medoxomil) एक सादी, तुरंत घुलने वाली गोली है, और जिन स्रोतों को मैंने देखा उनमें आपके शरीर के लिए कोई खास चेतावनी नहीं मिली, पर छोटी आंत कम होने से दवा कितनी सोखी जाएगी, यह पक्का नहीं कहा जा सकता।

why.claim: बेनिकार एक फिल्म-कोटेड गोली है, धीरे-धीरे या देर से निकलने वाली (एक्सटेंडेड/एंटेरिक-कोटेड) गोली नहीं।
ज़्यादातर दवाएं छोटी आंत के ऊपरी हिस्से (जेजुनम की शुरुआत) में सोखी जाती हैं, इसलिए वह हिस्सा बचा हो तो कई सादी, तुरंत घुलने वाली दवाएं सोखी जा सकती हैं।
सादी, जल्दी घुलने वाली गोलियों को स्टोमा वाले लोगों में कम जोखिम वाली श्रेणी में रखा गया है।
दवा कितनी सोखी जाएगी, यह स्टोमा के प्रकार से ज़्यादा बची हुई छोटी आंत की लंबाई और सेहत पर निर्भर करता है। आपकी छोटी आंत 100 सेमी से कम है।
आंत का हिस्सा निकाले जाने के बाद 37 में से 29 दवाओं का सोखना कम पाया गया, और 6 दवाओं का असर खत्म हो गया; यह हर दवा के लिए अलग होता है, इसलिए किसी एक व्यक्ति के लिए पहले से नहीं कहा जा सकता।

G:hong-2021#absorption-findings.text: Across studies reviewed, absorption was decreased for 29 of 37 drugs after intestinal resection, and 6 drugs lost clinical effect; the effect was drug-specific, so it cannot be turned into a single probability for one person.

G:remane-2025#formulation-classes.text: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).

G:sood-2013#residual-length.text: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

draft.verdict: जिन स्रोतों को मैंने देखा, उनमें आपकी इलियोस्टोमी के लिए Tricor गोली के खिलाफ़ कोई खास चेतावनी नहीं मिली। पर लेबल यह नहीं बताता कि यह आंत के किस हिस्से में सोखी जाती है, और यह पानी में लगभग घुलती ही नहीं, इसलिए फार्मासिस्ट से पूछना अच्छा रहेगा।

why.claim: लेबल में दवा का रूप 'TABLET' (गोली) लिखा है। यह धीरे-धीरे घुलने वाली या खास परत वाली गोली के रूप में नहीं लिखी है।
लेबल में यह नहीं लिखा कि दवा आंत के किस हिस्से में सोखी जाती है। लेबल सिर्फ़ इतना कहता है कि फेनोफाइब्रेट पानी में लगभग घुलता ही नहीं है।
ज़्यादातर दवाएं छोटी आंत के ऊपरी हिस्से में सोखी जाती हैं। जब यह हिस्सा बचा हो, तो कई सामान्य गोलियां सोखी जा सकती हैं।
स्टोमा वाले लोगों में सामान्य, जल्दी घुलने वाली गोलियों को कम जोखिम वाला माना गया है। धीरे-धीरे घुलने वाली और खास परत वाली दवाओं को ज़्यादा जोखिम वाला माना गया है।
दवा कितनी अच्छी तरह सोखी जाती है, यह स्टोमा के प्रकार से ज़्यादा इस पर निर्भर करता है कि छोटी आंत कितनी लंबी और कितनी स्वस्थ बची है।
आंत का हिस्सा निकाले जाने के बाद अध्ययनों में 37 में से 29 दवाओं का सोखना कम हुआ। यह असर हर दवा में अलग होता है, इसलिए किसी एक व्यक्ति के लिए पक्का नहीं कहा जा सकता।
लेबल कहता है कि Tricor दिन में एक बार, खाने के साथ या बिना, लें और हर गोली पूरी निगलें। कोई भी बदलाव फार्मासिस्ट या डॉक्टर का निर्णय है।
लेबल के विवरण में गोली में hypromellose, docusate sodium और sucrose जैसी चीज़ें लिखी हैं। बाकी सामग्री (inactive ingredients) वाला हिस्सा लेबल में नहीं मिला।
अगर दवा का उम्मीद के मुताबिक असर न दिखे, तो हो सकता है कि वह ठीक से सोखी नहीं जा रही। यह बात डॉक्टर या फार्मासिस्ट को बताएं।

final.verdict: जिन स्रोतों को मैंने देखा, उनमें आपकी इलियोस्टोमी के लिए Tricor गोली के खिलाफ़ कोई खास चेतावनी नहीं मिली। पर लेबल यह नहीं बताता कि यह आंत के किस हिस्से में सोखी जाती है, और यह पानी में लगभग घुलती ही नहीं, इसलिए फार्मासिस्ट से पूछना अच्छा रहेगा।

why.claim: लेबल में दवा का रूप 'TABLET' (गोली) लिखा है। यह धीरे-धीरे घुलने वाली या खास परत वाली गोली के रूप में नहीं लिखी है।
लेबल में यह नहीं लिखा कि दवा आंत के किस हिस्से में सोखी जाती है। लेबल सिर्फ़ इतना कहता है कि फेनोफाइब्रेट पानी में लगभग घुलता ही नहीं है।
ज़्यादातर दवाएं छोटी आंत के ऊपरी हिस्से में सोखी जाती हैं। जब यह हिस्सा बचा हो, तो कई सामान्य गोलियां सोखी जा सकती हैं।
स्टोमा वाले लोगों में सामान्य, जल्दी घुलने वाली गोलियों को कम जोखिम वाला माना गया है। धीरे-धीरे घुलने वाली और खास परत वाली दवाओं को ज़्यादा जोखिम वाला माना गया है।
दवा कितनी अच्छी तरह सोखी जाती है, यह स्टोमा के प्रकार से ज़्यादा इस पर निर्भर करता है कि छोटी आंत कितनी लंबी और कितनी स्वस्थ बची है।
आंत का हिस्सा निकाले जाने के बाद अध्ययनों में 37 में से 29 दवाओं का सोखना कम हुआ। यह असर हर दवा में अलग होता है, इसलिए किसी एक व्यक्ति के लिए पक्का नहीं कहा जा सकता।
लेबल कहता है कि Tricor दिन में एक बार, खाने के साथ या बिना, लें और हर गोली पूरी निगलें। कोई भी बदलाव फार्मासिस्ट या डॉक्टर का निर्णय है।
लेबल के विवरण में गोली में hypromellose, docusate sodium और sucrose जैसी चीज़ें लिखी हैं। बाकी सामग्री (inactive ingredients) वाला हिस्सा लेबल में नहीं मिला।
अगर दवा का उम्मीद के मुताबिक असर न दिखे, तो हो सकता है कि वह ठीक से सोखी नहीं जा रही। यह बात डॉक्टर या फार्मासिस्ट को बताएं।

evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.
evidence.G:hong-2021#absorption-findings: Across studies reviewed, absorption was decreased for 29 of 37 drugs after intestinal resection, and 6 drugs lost clinical effect; the effect was drug-specific, so it cannot be turned into a single probability for one person.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#malabsorption-suspect: If a medicine does not seem to produce its expected effect, malabsorption should be suspected and raised with the prescriber or pharmacist.
evidence.G:remane-2025#formulation-classes: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).
evidence.G:sood-2013#ileostomy-dehydration: People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium, and medicines such as diuretics and laxatives can add to that risk.
evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

why.claim: Comprimidos de liberação prolongada e com revestimento entérico estão entre os mais arriscados para quem tem estomia. Comprimidos simples, que se dissolvem rápido, ficam entre os de menor risco. Sem saber que tipo de comprimido é o AG-X, não dá para dizer em qual grupo ele entra.
Sem o cólon, os produtos de liberação lenta têm menos tempo e menos espaço no intestino para liberar o remédio.
A absorção dos remédios depende mais do comprimento e da saúde do intestino delgado que ficou do que do tipo de estomia. Você tem mais de 200 cm de intestino delgado.
Quem tem ileostomia corre mais risco de desidratação e de sódio baixo. Alguns remédios, como diuréticos e laxantes, podem aumentar esse risco.

Guidelines: AGA SBS update, Practical Gastroenterology #139, Sood 2013, Parrish & DiBaise 2017
draft.verdict: నేను చూసిన మూలాల్లో లేబెటలాల్ హైడ్రోక్లోరైడ్ మామూలు (వెంటనే కరిగే) మాత్ర మీ శరీరానికి పనిచేయదు అని చెప్పే విషయం ఏదీ దొరకలేదు. కానీ లేబెల్ వివరాలు పూర్తిగా అందలేదు, అందుకే మీ ఫార్మసిస్ట్‌ను అడగండి.

why.claim: ఇది మాత్ర (టాబ్లెట్) రూపంలో ఉంది. ఇది వెంటనే కరిగే రకం. నెమ్మదిగా కరిగే రకం కాదు.
చాలా మందులు చిన్న ప్రేగు మొదటి భాగంలోనే శోషించబడతాయి. అందుకే ఆ భాగం మిగిలి ఉంటే చాలా మామూలు మాత్రలు ఇంకా శోషించబడగలవు.
మందు ఎంత బాగా శోషించబడుతుంది అనేది మిగిలిన చిన్న ప్రేగు పొడవు, ఆరోగ్యం మీద ఆధారపడి ఉంటుంది. మీకు 100 సెం.మీ. కంటే తక్కువ ఉంది కాబట్టి ఇది అడగాల్సిన విషయం.
మాత్రల కంటే ద్రవ రూప మందులు కొన్నిసార్లు బాగా శోషించబడతాయి. కానీ వాటిలో తరచుగా షుగర్ ఆల్కహాల్స్ ఉంటాయి, అవి మలం ఎక్కువ చేయగలవు.

careTeamAnswers.summary: Rapporté par un autre utilisateur, d'après sa propre équipe de soins : sa diététicienne lui a expliqué que sans côlon, l'eau plate peut faire perdre du sel et faire monter le débit.

swapToAskAbout.text: Une solution de réhydratation orale, à la place d'une partie de l'eau : c'est une idée à proposer à votre équipe. 2 personnes l'ont publiée comme remplacement de l'eau (aucune avec votre type de stomie), et un soignant l'a approuvée.

draft.verdict: L'eau gazeuse est une eau pauvre en sel. Avec une iléostomie sans côlon, ce type de boisson mérite qu'on en parle avec votre équipe, car les sources signalent un risque de déshydratation et de manque de sel.

why.claim: Les personnes avec une iléostomie ont un risque plus élevé de déshydratation et de manque de sel (sodium).

Quand l'intestin s'arrête au jéjunum (stomie haute), l'eau plate et les autres boissons pauvres en sel peuvent attirer le sel dans l'intestin et faire monter le débit de la stomie. On les limite donc souvent au profit d'une solution de réhydratation orale. Cette règle est écrite pour une stomie plus haute que la vôtre. Il faut donc demander à votre équipe si elle s'applique à vous.
Une solution de réhydratation orale (sucre + sels) est la boisson conseillée pour remplacer l'eau et le sel perdus en cas de grêle court.
Pour le grêle court, on cite en général des solutions contenant environ 90 à 120 mmol/L de sodium. C'est plus que beaucoup de boissons de réhydratation vendues dans le commerce.
On conseille en général de boire par petites gorgées tout au long de la journée plutôt qu'en grande quantité d'un coup. Beaucoup d'équipes conseillent aussi de boire à distance des repas.
La soif, des urines foncées ou plus rares, des vertiges en se levant et un débit de stomie qui augmente sont des signes de déshydratation. Il faut les signaler vite à votre équipe.
Parmi les personnes avec une iléostomie qui ont noté l'eau, 6 sur 13 disent qu'elle leur a fait du mal, 5 n'ont rien remarqué et 2 disent qu'elle les a aidées.

G:aga-sbs#fluids-sipping.text: Fluids are generally sipped through the day rather than taken in large amounts at once, and many teams suggest separating drinks from meals.

G:sood-2013#ileostomy-dehydration.text: People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium, and medicines such as diuretics and laxatives can add to that risk.
