evidence.G:aga-sbs#dehydration-signs: Thirst, dark or reduced urine, dizziness on standing, and rising stoma output are warning signs of dehydration that should be raised with the care team promptly.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#diet-simple-sugars: Concentrated simple sugars (sweets, syrups, sweetened drinks) draw water into the bowel and are generally limited in short bowel syndrome.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#fluids-hypertonic: Hypertonic, sugary drinks such as fruit juice and regular soda pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output or diarrhea in short bowel syndrome; they are best limited regardless of anatomy.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#fluids-ors: A glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink to replace fluid and sodium losses in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#fluids-sipping: Fluids are generally sipped through the day rather than taken in large amounts at once, and many teams suggest separating drinks from meals.
evidence.G:pd-2017#caffeine-alcohol: Caffeine and alcohol can increase output and fluid losses and are usually limited in short bowel syndrome.
evidence.G:pd-2017#ors-sodium: For short bowel syndrome, oral rehydration solutions with a sodium concentration of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are generally recommended; this is higher than many commercial rehydration drinks.
evidence.G:pd-2017#salt: Salting food and choosing salty snacks is commonly encouraged in short bowel syndrome with high output, within the care team's advice for the person's heart and kidney health.
evidence.G:pd-2017#sports-drinks: Typical sports drinks are low in sodium and high in sugar compared with an SBS oral rehydration solution, so they are not a substitute for it.
evidence.G:pg139#sugar-alcohols: Sorbitol, xylitol, mannitol and other sugar alcohols are poorly absorbed, draw water into the gut, and can raise stoma output or diarrhea; they are common inactive ingredients in liquid medicines and sugar-free products.
evidence.G:sood-2013#ileostomy-dehydration: People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium, and medicines such as diuretics and laxatives can add to that risk.
evidence.G:who-ors#purpose: Oral rehydration solution works because glucose and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel, carrying water with them.
evidence.G:who-ors#reduced-osmolarity-composition: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (2003) contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L (total 245 mOsm/L). It was designed for acute diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.

diagram.label: Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel

draft.verdict: No encontré ningún problema concreto en las fuentes que revisé, pero tampoco hay datos que confirmen que el fenofibrato se absorbe bien con su intestino corto. Eso solo se puede saber en su caso con su equipo médico.

why.claim: La etiqueta indica la forma solo como 'tableta'. No menciona liberación prolongada ni retardada.
Las tabletas de liberación prolongada o con capa entérica suelen evitarse tras una resección grande del intestino. Eso no aparece en esta etiqueta.
La mayoría de los medicamentos se absorben en la parte alta del intestino delgado. Por eso muchas tabletas normales se pueden absorber si esa parte sigue ahí.
Qué tan bien se absorbe un medicamento depende sobre todo del largo y la salud del intestino que queda.
En estudios con personas operadas del intestino, 29 de 37 medicamentos se absorbieron menos. Depende de cada medicamento y no se puede predecir para una persona.
La etiqueta dice que el fenofibrato casi no se disuelve en agua. Por eso no se pudo medir del todo cuánto absorbe el cuerpo.
La etiqueta dice que se toma una vez al día, con o sin comida, y que la tableta se traga entera.
Entre los ingredientes, la etiqueta nombra hipromelosa, docusato de sodio y sacarosa. No encontré la lista completa de ingredientes inactivos.
Nadie ha registrado todavía cómo le fue con el fenofibrato, ni con su tipo de estoma ni con otros.

Slow-release products may let out part of their dose in the colon. Without a colon, they get less time and less surface to do that. Your parent's colon is not connected.
How well pills are absorbed depends most on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is.
Crushing an extended-release product defeats its design and can be dangerous. Whether to change how a medicine is taken is the pharmacist's decision.
If you ever see a whole tablet or shell in the pouch, show the pharmacist. It may mean the pill did not dissolve, or it may be an empty shell. It is not proof either way.

draft.verdict: لم أجد شيئًا في المصادر التي راجعتها يمنع نيورونتين (غابابنتين) أقراصًا سريعة الإطلاق مع فغرتك اللفائفية. لكن المصادر لا تتحدث عن هذا الدواء تحديدًا، وقد يكون امتصاصه أقل بعد استئصال جزء من الأمعاء.

why.claim: قرصك سريع الإطلاق، أي ليس ممتد الإطلاق.
كيف يمتصه الجسم: معظم الأدوية تُمتص في الجزء العلوي من الأمعاء الدقيقة. لذلك يمكن أن تُمتص كثير من الأقراص العادية سريعة الإطلاق إذا بقي هذا الجزء.
تقول النشرة إن الجسم يمتص نسبة أقل من الغابابنتين كلما زادت الجرعة اليومية. وهذه معلومة عامة عن الدواء، وليست خاصة بالفغرة.
الأقراص العادية سريعة الذوبان تُعدّ من الأشكال «غير الحرجة» عند مرضى الفغرة. أما الأشكال ممتدة الإطلاق والمغلفة معويًا فتُعدّ «حرجة».

عادةً يُتجنَّب الدواء ممتد الإطلاق أو متأخر الإطلاق بعد استئصال جزء كبير من الأمعاء الدقيقة. والسبب أنه يحتاج إلى مرور طويل وطبيعي في الأمعاء حتى يخرج منه الدواء. إذا تغيّر شكل الدواء الذي تأخذه يومًا ما، فهذه نقطة تستحق السؤال عنها.
مدى امتصاص الأدوية يعتمد على طول ما بقي من الأمعاء الدقيقة وصحته، أكثر مما يعتمد على نوع الفغرة.
في الدراسات، قلّ امتصاص كثير من الأدوية بعد استئصال جزء من الأمعاء. لكن هذا يختلف من دواء لآخر، ولا يمكن تحويله إلى نسبة محددة لشخص واحد.
إذا كان الدواء قد لا يُمتص جيدًا، فقد يفكر الفريق الطبي في شكل آخر من الدواء نفسه، مثل الشكل السائل أو الذي يذوب.
الأدوية السائلة قد تُمتص بشكل أوثق من الأقراص الصلبة. لكنها كثيرًا ما تحتوي على كحولات سكرية قد تزيد كمية الخارج من الفغرة.
في بيانات المنتج المتاحة، المكونات المذكورة غير الغابابنتين هي نشا الذرة والكوبوفيدون فقط، ولا يوجد سوربيتول. قسم المكونات غير الفعالة الكامل لم يكن متاحًا.
مرضى الفغرة اللفائفية أكثر عرضة للجفاف ونقص الصوديوم.

why.claim: The Ecotrin (enteric-coated aspirin) label lists it as a delayed-release tablet.
Coated and delayed-release tablets are made to get past the stomach before they dissolve. When food moves through quickly, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets come out whole.
After a large part of the small bowel has been removed, doctors usually avoid slow-release and coated medicines because they need a long, normal trip through the gut to release the drug.
The tramadol label lists a plain tablet, not a slow-release or coated one.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel, so many plain tablets can still be absorbed if that part is still there.
The tramadol label says that on average about 75% of a dose taken by mouth reaches the blood. That figure is for people in general, not people with short bowel syndrome.

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask your pharmacist whether an immediate-release or liquid version of memantine would suit your anatomy better than the extended-release capsule.

draft.verdict: Whether to open this capsule is a decision for your pharmacist, because the label says not to divide, chew or crush it, and with your short bowel the extended-release design itself is a concern.

why.claim: The label says memantine extended-release capsules should not be divided, chewed, or crushed.
This product is an extended-release capsule.

Breaking open the design of an extended-release product defeats how it is meant to work and can be dangerous. Crushing or dissolving to help absorption is only discussed for plain immediate-release tablets, and even then it is the pharmacist's decision.
Guidelines say to check with a pharmacist before changing how you take a medicine, such as crushing, splitting or switching products.
Time-release medicines need enough time in the small bowel to let out their drug. With a shorter bowel or fast transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
Slow-release products may rely on the colon for part of their release. Without a colon, they have less time and less surface to release the drug.
Extended-release products are generally avoided after a large bowel resection. An immediate-release or liquid version of the same drug is often worth asking the pharmacist about.
The label says how much memantine the body takes in is the same whether this capsule is taken with food or on an empty stomach.

draft.verdict: هذا قرار يعود للصيدلي أو الطبيب، لكن الملصق يقول إن هذا القرص لا يُقسم ولا يُسحق، والإرشادات تقول إن سحق الأقراص ممتدة المفعول يُفسد طريقة عملها وقد يكون خطيراً.

why.claim: الملصق يقول إن أقراص الميترونيدازول ممتدة المفعول يجب ألا تُقسم أو تُمضغ أو تُسحق.
شكل هذا الدواء على الملصق هو قرص مغلّف ممتد المفعول.

الإرشادات تقول إن السحق أو الإذابة قد يساعدان على الامتصاص فقط في الأقراص العادية فورية المفعول، وهذا قرار للصيدلي. أما سحق الأقراص ممتدة المفعول أو المغلّفة معوياً فيُفسد طريقة عملها وقد يكون خطيراً.
الإرشادات تنصح باستشارة الصيدلي قبل تغيير شكل الدواء، مثل السحق أو التقسيم أو التبديل إلى منتج آخر.
الأدوية ممتدة المفعول تحتاج إلى وقت كافٍ في الأمعاء الدقيقة لتُطلق الدواء. ومع أمعاء أقصر أو مرور سريع، قد يخرج جزء من الجرعة من الجسم قبل أن يُطلق.
الأدوية بطيئة الإطلاق قد تُطلق جزءاً من جرعتها في القولون. وبدون قولون يكون أمامها وقت ومساحة أقل لتُطلق الدواء.
الأدوية ممتدة المفعول يُتجنَّب استخدامها عادةً بعد استئصال جزء كبير من الأمعاء. والسؤال عن نسخة فورية المفعول أو سائلة من نفس الدواء غالباً ما يستحق أن تطرحه على الصيدلي.
معظم الأدوية تُمتص في الجزء العلوي من الأمعاء الدقيقة، لذلك كثير من الأدوية العادية فورية المفعول يمكن أن تُمتص ما دام هذا الجزء موجوداً.

draft.ask: ASK: La notice interdit d'écraser Envarsus XR ; avec mon iléostomie sans côlon, existe-t-il une forme de tacrolimus mieux adaptée à mon intestin ?

diagram.label: Slow-release products can rely on the colon for part of their release

swapToAskAbout.text: Plutôt que d'écraser le comprimé, demandez à votre pharmacien ou à votre prescripteur si une forme classée « non critique », comme une forme qui se dissout vite, pourrait être envisagée pour vous. C'est leur décision.

draft.verdict: Écraser Envarsus XR est une décision pour votre pharmacien ou votre prescripteur : la notice dit d'avaler les comprimés entiers sans les écraser, et les guides conseillent de demander au pharmacien avant de changer la forme d'un médicament.

why.claim: La notice dit d'avaler les comprimés entiers avec de l'eau, sans les mâcher, les couper, les écraser ni les dissoudre.
Les guides disent de demander à un pharmacien avant de changer la forme d'un médicament, par exemple l'écraser, le couper ou changer de produit.
Envarsus XR est un comprimé à libération prolongée.

Votre inquiétude est légitime. Les médicaments à libération prolongée ont besoin d'assez de temps dans l'intestin pour libérer leur contenu. Si le transit est plus court ou plus rapide, une partie de la dose peut sortir avant d'avoir été libérée.
Les produits à libération lente peuvent libérer une partie de leur dose dans le côlon. Sans côlon, ils ont moins de temps et de surface pour le faire.

Chez les personnes avec une stomie, les formes à libération prolongée sont classées « critiques » pour la dissolution. Les solutions et les comprimés simples qui se dissolvent vite sont « non critiques ».
L'absorption des médicaments dépend surtout de la longueur et de l'état de l'intestin grêle restant, plus que du type de stomie.

draft.verdict: Whether to crush or cut Envarsus XR is a decision for your pharmacist or transplant team, not something to try on your own: the label says to swallow it whole, the guidelines warn that crushing extended-release tablets can be dangerous, and your low levels are worth raising with them soon.

why.claim: Envarsus XR is an extended-release tablet.
The label says to swallow the tablets whole with fluid, preferably water, and not to chew, divide, crush or dissolve them.

Crushing extended-release products defeats how they are designed to work and can be dangerous. Crushing is only discussed for plain immediate-release tablets, and even then it is the pharmacist's decision.
Patients should talk to a pharmacist before changing how they take a medicine, such as crushing, splitting or switching products.
Time-release tablets need enough time in the small bowel. With a shorter bowel or fast transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
Slow-release products may release part of their dose in the large intestine. Without the colon in use, as with your ileostomy, they have less time and surface to release.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, sustained-release and delayed-release medicines are generally avoided.

For drugs where the right amount is a narrow range, clinicians may check blood levels or watch the effect closely, because absorption after bowel surgery is hard to predict. Your low levels are exactly the kind of result to bring to them.

The label says that in healthy people, this tablet's bioavailability was higher than with tacrolimus immediate-release and extended-release capsules. So any switch between forms needs your team to work out the dose.

why.claim: This product is an extended-release tablet.
The label says to swallow the tablets whole, without crushing, chewing or sucking.

Crushing an extended-release or coated product defeats how it is designed to work, and it can be dangerous. Crushing is only considered for plain immediate-release tablets, and that is the pharmacist's decision.
Patients should talk to a pharmacist before changing the form of a medicine, such as crushing it, splitting it or switching products.

After a large part of the small bowel is removed, extended-release products are usually avoided. Asking the pharmacist about an immediate-release or liquid version of the same drug is often worthwhile.
Time-release tablets need enough time in the small bowel. When the bowel is shorter or moves fast, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
Slow-release products can release part of their dose in the colon. Without a colon, they have less time and less surface to do that.
Sugary drinks like fruit juice pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output. Guidelines say to limit them.
Liquid medicines may absorb more reliably than tablets in short bowel syndrome. But they often contain sugar alcohols, which can raise stoma output.
Of 12 people with an end-jejunostomy who logged this tablet, 6 said it helped, 3 saw no change, and 3 said it hurt.

why.claim: Si una medicina no parece hacer el efecto esperado, las guías dicen que puede ser un problema de absorción y que hay que hablarlo con quien la recetó o con el farmacéutico.
KAPSPARGO es una cápsula de liberación prolongada.

Las medicinas de liberación prolongada necesitan suficiente tiempo en el intestino delgado para soltar el medicamento. Si el tránsito es rápido o el intestino es más corto, parte de la dosis puede salir del cuerpo antes de soltarse.
Estas medicinas pueden soltar parte de la dosis en el colon. Sin colon, tienen menos tiempo y superficie para hacerlo.
Qué tan bien se absorben las medicinas depende más del largo y la salud del intestino delgado que queda que del tipo de estoma.

Un estudio pone las medicinas de liberación prolongada en el grupo de riesgo "crítico" para personas con ostomía, y los líquidos y las tabletas simples que se disuelven rápido en el grupo "no crítico".
La etiqueta dice que KAPSPARGO Sprinkle se debe tragar entero.
De 13 personas con ileostomía que registraron esta medicina, 3 dijeron que les funcionó bien, 6 que no notaron nada y 4 que les fue mal. Son reportes personales, no un estudio.

final.verdict: No le puedo decir cuántas cápsulas tomar ni si tomar una más: eso lo decide su médico o farmacéutico, y las guías dicen que, si cree que una medicina no le hace efecto, se lo diga a ellos.

why.claim: Si una medicina no parece hacer el efecto esperado, las guías dicen que puede ser un problema de absorción y que hay que hablarlo con quien la recetó o con el farmacéutico.
KAPSPARGO es una cápsula de liberación prolongada.

Las medicinas de liberación prolongada necesitan suficiente tiempo en el intestino delgado para soltar el medicamento. Si el tránsito es rápido o el intestino es más corto, parte de la dosis puede salir del cuerpo antes de soltarse.
Estas medicinas pueden soltar parte de la dosis en el colon. Sin colon, tienen menos tiempo y superficie para hacerlo.
Qué tan bien se absorben las medicinas depende más del largo y la salud del intestino delgado que queda que del tipo de estoma.

Un estudio pone las medicinas de liberación prolongada en el grupo de riesgo "crítico" para personas con ostomía, y los líquidos y las tabletas simples que se disuelven rápido en el grupo "no crítico".
La etiqueta dice que KAPSPARGO Sprinkle se debe tragar entero.
De 13 personas con ileostomía que registraron esta medicina, 3 dijeron que les funcionó bien, 6 que no notaron nada y 4 que les fue mal. Son reportes personales, no un estudio.

swapToAskAbout.text: If it isn't absorbing well, you could ask your care team whether another form of furosemide, including a non-oral form, might suit you better.

draft.verdict: I can't tell you how much to take, because that is a decision for your prescriber, but if your furosemide solution doesn't seem to be working, the guidelines say to bring it up with your prescriber or pharmacist as a possible absorption problem.

why.claim: If a medicine doesn't seem to have its expected effect, it may not be absorbing well. That should be raised with the prescriber or pharmacist.
After part of the bowel is removed, absorption changes differently for each drug. So there is no single rule for how one person absorbs a medicine.
How well medicines absorb depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left, more than on the type of stoma.
In healthy fasting men, the solution absorbed about as well as the tablet (60% vs 64% of an IV dose). The label checked doesn't give figures for people with a stoma.
People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium. Diuretics like furosemide can add to that risk.
The label lists sorbitol solution as an inactive ingredient.
Sorbitol is poorly absorbed, pulls water into the gut and can raise stoma output.
If a medicine may be poorly absorbed, the care team may consider other forms of the same drug, such as non-oral forms.
Thirst, dark urine or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, and rising stoma output are warning signs of dehydration. Tell your care team about them promptly.

draft.verdict: How many cephalexin capsules to take is up to your prescriber or pharmacist, not me, and nothing I checked shows how much of it your body takes in.

why.claim: How many capsules to take is a decision for your prescriber or pharmacist. Please don't change your dose on your own.
Studies found that many medicines are absorbed less after part of the bowel is removed. But it differs from drug to drug, so no one can predict it for one person from general rules.
How well a medicine is absorbed depends mostly on how much healthy small bowel is left.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel. So many plain immediate-release medicines can still be absorbed when that part is still there.
The label I could find is for cephalexin tablets, not capsules. It says they are acid stable and can be taken with or without food.
That label had no pharmacokinetics section, so I could not see where in the gut cephalexin is absorbed or how much.
Liquid medicines may be absorbed more reliably than solid ones in short bowel syndrome. But liquids often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.

why.claim: This medicine is an extended-release tablet.
The label says to swallow these tablets whole. It says not to cut, crush or chew them.
When the bowel is short or food moves through fast, part of a time-release dose may leave the body before the drug is released.
Slow-release products may release part of their dose in the large intestine (colon). Without a colon, they have less time and less surface to release the drug.

After a large part of the small bowel is removed, it is hard to predict how much of a medicine gets absorbed. For some medicines, clinicians may check blood levels or watch closely how well the medicine is working.
How well medicines are absorbed depends mostly on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is.
If a medicine doesn't seem to be working as expected, poor absorption could be the reason, and that is worth raising with your prescriber or pharmacist.
Asking the pharmacist about an immediate-release or liquid version of the same medicine is often worthwhile.
Liquid medicines may be absorbed more reliably, but they often contain sugar alcohols, which can increase stoma output.

why.claim: This is a delayed-release tablet.
The tablets have an enteric coating.
The label says to swallow these tablets whole, not crushed or chewed. Any change is up to your pharmacist or prescriber.
A study of people with an ostomy put enteric-coated and extended-release products in its 'critical' group. Those are the ones most likely to have trouble dissolving.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there, and medicines are often absorbed normally. But the type of stoma alone doesn't guarantee it.
How well medicines get absorbed depends more on how long and healthy the rest of the small bowel is than on the type of stoma.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel.

If you ever see what looks like a whole tablet or shell in your pouch, the medicine may not have dissolved. Or it may be an empty shell left after the medicine came out. It isn't proof either way, but show your pharmacist.
In that study, more than 60% of the ostomy patients interviewed said no one had told them how an ostomy can affect their medicines.

G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio.text: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.

G:remane-2025#formulation-classes.text: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).

G:remane-2025#tablet-in-pouch.text: An intact tablet or shell seen in the pouch can mean the medicine did not dissolve, or it can be an empty shell left after the drug was released. It is worth showing the pharmacist; it is not proof either way.

G:sood-2013#colostomy.text: With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually intact and oral medicines are often absorbed normally; but the stoma type alone does not tell you remaining small-bowel length, so it is not a guarantee.

G:sood-2013#residual-length.text: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.

evidence.L:boxed_warning: WARNING: LIFE THREATENING ADVERSE REACTIONS WARNING: LIFE THREATENING ADVERSE REACTIONS See full prescribing information for complete boxed warning. Hepatotoxicity, including fatalities, usually during the first 6 months of treatment. Children under the age of two years and patients with mitochondrial disorders are at higher risk. Monitor patients closely, and perform serum liver testing prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter ( 5.1 ) Fetal Risk, particularly neural tube defects, other major malformations, and decreased IQ ( 5.2 , 5.3 , 5.4 ) Pancreatitis, including fatal hemorrhagic cases ( 5.5 ) Hepatotoxicity General Population: Hepatic failure resulting in fatalities has occurred in patients receiving valproate and its derivatives. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment. Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. Children under the age of two years are at a considerably increased risk of developing fatal hepatotoxicity, especially those on multiple anticonvulsants, those with congenital metabolic disorders, those with severe seizure disorders accompanied by mental retardation, and those with organic brain disease. When divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets are used in this patient group, it should be used with extreme caution and as a sole agent. The benefits of therapy should be weighed against the risks. The incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases considerably in progressively older patient groups. Patients with Mitochondrial Disease: There is an increased risk of valproate-induced acute liver failure and resultant deaths in patients with hereditary neurometabolic syndromes caused by DNA mutations of the mitochondrial DNA Polymerase γ (POLG) gene (e.g., Alpers Huttenlocher Syndrome). Divalproex sodium is contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder [see Contraindications ( 4 )] . In patients over two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a hereditary mitochondrial disease, divalproex sodium should only be used after other anticonvulsants have failed. This older group of patients should be closely monitored during treatment with divalproex sodium for the development of acute liver injury with regular clinical assessments and serum liver testing. POLG mutation screening should be performed in accordance with current clinical practice [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. Fetal Risk Valproate can cause major congenital malformations, particularly neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida). In addition, valproate can cause decreased IQ scores and neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure. Valproate is therefore contraindicated for prophylaxis of migraine headaches in pregnant women and in women of childbearing potential who are not using effective contraception [see Contraindications ( 4 )]. Valproate should not be used to treat women with epilepsy or bipolar disorder who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. Valproate should not be administered to a woman of childbearing potential unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. evidence.L:clinical_pharmacology: 12 CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY 12.1 Mechanism of Action Divalproex sodium dissociates to the valproate ion in the gastrointestinal tract. The mechanisms by which valproate exerts its therapeutic effects have not been established. It has been suggested that its activity in epilepsy is related to increased brain concentrations of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). 12.2 Pharmacodynamics The relationship between plasma concentration and clinical response is not well documented. One contributing factor is the nonlinear, concentration dependent protein binding of valproate which affects the clearance of the drug. Thus, monitoring of total serum valproate cannot provide a reliable index of the bioactive valproate species. For example, because the plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent, the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Higher than expected free fractions occur in the elderly, in hyperlipidemic patients, and in patients with hepatic and renal diseases. Epilepsy The therapeutic range in epilepsy is commonly considered to be 50 to 100 mcg/mL of total valproate, although some patients may be controlled with lower or higher plasma concentrations. Mania In placebo-controlled clinical trials of acute mania, patients were dosed to clinical response with trough plasma concentrations between 50 and 125 mcg/mL [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.1 )]. 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption/Bioavailability Equivalent oral doses of divalproex sodium products and valproic acid capsules deliver equivalent quantities of valproate ion systemically. Although the rate of valproate ion absorption may vary with the formulation administered (liquid, solid, or sprinkle), conditions of use (e.g., fasting or postprandial) and the method of administration (e.g., whether the contents of the capsule are sprinkled on food or the capsule is taken intact), these differences should be of minor clinical importance under the steady state conditions achieved in chronic use in the treatment of epilepsy. However, it is possible that differences among the various valproate products in T max and C max could be important upon initiation of treatment. For example, in single dose studies, the effect of feeding had a greater influence on the rate of absorption of the tablet (increase in T max from 4 to 8 hours) than on the absorption of the sprinkle capsules (increase in T max from 3.3 to 4.8 hours). While the absorption rate from the G.I. tract and fluctuation in valproate plasma concentrations vary with dosing regimen and formulation, the efficacy of valproate as an anticonvulsant in chronic use is unlikely to be affected. Experience employing dosing regimens from once-a-day to four-times-a-day, as well as studies in primate epilepsy models involving constant rate infusion, indicate that total daily systemic bioavailability (extent of absorption) is the primary determinant of seizure control and that differences in the ratios of plasma peak to trough concentrations between valproate formulations are inconsequential from a practical clinical standpoint. Whether or not rate of absorption influences the efficacy of valproate as an antimanic or antimigraine agent is unknown. Co-administration of oral valproate products with food and substitution among the various divalproex sodium and valproic acid formulations should cause no clinical problems in the management of patients with epilepsy [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.2 )] . Nonetheless, any changes in dosage administration, or the addition or discontinuance of concomitant drugs should ordinarily be accompanied by close monitoring of clinical status and valproate plasma concentrations. evidence.L:description: 11 DESCRIPTION Divalproex sodium is a stable co-ordination compound comprised of sodium valproate and valproic acid in a 1:1 molar relationship and formed during the partial neutralization of valproic acid with 0.5 equivalent of sodium hydroxide. Chemically it is designated as sodium hydrogen bis(2-propylpentanoate). Divalproex sodium has the following structure: Divalproex sodium occurs as a white powder with a characteristic odor. Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets USP are for oral administration. Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets USP are supplied in three dosage strengths containing divalproex sodium equivalent to 125 mg, 250 mg, or 500 mg of valproic acid. Inactive Ingredients Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets USP: colloidal silicon dioxide, D&C Red No. 30, FD&C Blue No. 2, hydroxylpropyl cellulose, hypromellose, hypromellose phthalate, iron oxide black, iron oxide yellow, low substituted hydroxypropyl cellulose, magnesium stearate, microcrystalline cellulose, pregelatinised starch, propylene glycol, shellac, talc, titanium dioxide, triethyl citrate. evidence.L:dosage_and_administration: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets are administered orally in divided doses. Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets should be swallowed whole and should not be crushed or chewed ( 2.1 , 2.2 ). Mania: Initial dose is 750 mg daily, increasing as rapidly as possible to achieve therapeutic response or desired plasma level ( 2.1 ). The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day ( 2.1 , 2.2 ). Complex Partial Seizures: Start at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day to achieve optimal clinical response; if response is not satisfactory, check valproate plasma level; see full prescribing information for conversion to monotherapy ( 2.2 ). The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day ( 2.1 , 2.2 ). Absence Seizures: Start at 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day until seizure control or limiting side effects ( 2.2 ). The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day ( 2.1 , 2.2 ). Migraine: The recommended starting dose is 250 mg twice daily, thereafter increasing to a maximum of 1,000 mg/day as needed ( 2.3 ). Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets are intended for oral administration. Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets should be swallowed whole and should not be crushed or chewed. Patients should be informed to take divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets every day as prescribed. If a dose is missed it should be taken as soon as possible, unless it is almost time for the next dose. If a dose is skipped, the patient should not double the next dose. 2.1 Mania Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets are administered orally. The recommended initial dose is 750 mg daily in divided doses. The dose should be increased as rapidly as possible to achieve the lowest therapeutic dose which produces the desired clinical effect or the desired range of plasma concentrations. In placebo-controlled clinical trials of acute mania, patients were dosed to a clinical response with a trough plasma concentration between 50 and 125 mcg/mL. Maximum concentrations were generally achieved within 14 days. The maximum recommended dosage is 60 mg/kg/day. There is no body of evidence available from controlled trials to guide a clinician in the longer term management of a patient who improves during divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets treatment of an acute manic episode. While it is generally agreed that pharmacological treatment beyond an acute response in mania is desirable, both for maintenance of the initial response and for prevention of new manic episodes, there are no data to support the benefits of divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets in such longer-term treatment. Although there are no efficacy data that specifically address longer-term antimanic treatment with divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets, the safety of divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets in long-term use is supported by data from record reviews involving approximately 360 patients treated with divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets for greater than 3 months. 2.2 Epilepsy Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets are administered orally. Divalproex sodium delayed-release tablets are indicated as monotherapy and adjunctive therapy in complex partial seizures in adults and pediatric patients down to the age of 10 years, and in simple and complex absence seizures. evidence.L:pharmacokinetics: 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption/Bioavailability Equivalent oral doses of divalproex sodium products and valproic acid capsules deliver equivalent quantities of valproate ion systemically. Although the rate of valproate ion absorption may vary with the formulation administered (liquid, solid, or sprinkle), conditions of use (e.g., fasting or postprandial) and the method of administration (e.g., whether the contents of the capsule are sprinkled on food or the capsule is taken intact), these differences should be of minor clinical importance under the steady state conditions achieved in chronic use in the treatment of epilepsy. However, it is possible that differences among the various valproate products in T max and C max could be important upon initiation of treatment. For example, in single dose studies, the effect of feeding had a greater influence on the rate of absorption of the tablet (increase in T max from 4 to 8 hours) than on the absorption of the sprinkle capsules (increase in T max from 3.3 to 4.8 hours). While the absorption rate from the G.I. tract and fluctuation in valproate plasma concentrations vary with dosing regimen and formulation, the efficacy of valproate as an anticonvulsant in chronic use is unlikely to be affected. Experience employing dosing regimens from once-a-day to four-times-a-day, as well as studies in primate epilepsy models involving constant rate infusion, indicate that total daily systemic bioavailability (extent of absorption) is the primary determinant of seizure control and that differences in the ratios of plasma peak to trough concentrations between valproate formulations are inconsequential from a practical clinical standpoint. Whether or not rate of absorption influences the efficacy of valproate as an antimanic or antimigraine agent is unknown. Co-administration of oral valproate products with food and substitution among the various divalproex sodium and valproic acid formulations should cause no clinical problems in the management of patients with epilepsy [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.2 )] . Nonetheless, any changes in dosage administration, or the addition or discontinuance of concomitant drugs should ordinarily be accompanied by close monitoring of clinical status and valproate plasma concentrations. Distribution Protein Binding: The plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent and the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Protein binding of valproate is reduced in the elderly, in patients with chronic hepatic diseases, in patients with renal impairment, and in the presence of other drugs (e.g., aspirin). Conversely, valproate may displace certain protein-bound drugs (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine, warfarin, and tolbutamide) [see Drug Interactions ( 7.2 ) for more detailed information on the pharmacokinetic interactions of valproate with other drugs]. CNS Distribution: Valproate concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) approximate unbound concentrations in plasma (about 10% of total concentration). Metabolism Valproate is metabolized almost entirely by the liver. In adult patients on monotherapy, 30 to 50% of an administered dose appears in urine as a glucuronide conjugate. Mitochondrial β-oxidation is the other major metabolic pathway, typically accounting for over 40% of the dose. Usually, less than 15 to 20% of the dose is eliminated by other oxidative mechanisms. Less than 3% of an administered dose is excreted unchanged in urine. The relationship between dose and total valproate concentration is nonlinear; concentration does not increase proportionally with the dose, but rather, increases to a lesser extent due to saturable plasma protein binding. The kinetics of unbound drug are linear. Elimination Mean plasma clearance and volume of distribution for total valproate are 0.56 L/hr/1.73 m 2 and 11 L/1.73 m 2 , respectively. Mean plasma clearance and volume of distribution for free valproate are 4.6 L/hr

evidence.L:warnings_and_cautions: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Birth defects, decreased IQ, and neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure: Should not be used to treat women with epilepsy or bipolar disorder who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant or to treat a woman of childbearing potential unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable ( 5.2 , 5.3 , 5.4 ) Pancreatitis: Divalproex sodium should ordinarily be discontinued ( 5.5 ) Suicidal behavior or ideation: Antiepileptic drugs, including divalproex sodium, increase the risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior ( 5.7 ) Bleeding and other hematopoietic disorders: Monitor platelet counts and coagulation tests ( 5.8 ) Hyperammonemia and hyperammonemic encephalopathy: Measure ammonia level if unexplained lethargy and vomiting or changes in mental status, and also with concomitant topiramate use; consider discontinuation of valproate therapy ( 5.6 , 5.9 , 5.10 ) Hypothermia: Hypothermia has been reported during valproate therapy with occur in patients using concomitant topiramate ( 5.11 ) Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)/Multiorgan Hypersensitivity Reaction; serious dermatologic reactions, and angioedema: Discontinue divalproex sodium unless an alternate etiology is established ( 4 , 5.12 , 5.13 , 5.14 ) 5.1 Hepatotoxicity General Information on Hepatotoxicity Hepatic failure resulting in fatalities has occurred in patients receiving valproate. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment. Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months of valproate therapy. However, healthcare providers should not rely totally on serum biochemistry since these tests may not be abnormal in all instances, but should also consider the results of careful interim medical history and physical examination. Caution should be observed when administering valproate products to patients with a prior history of hepatic disease. why.claim: O rótulo diz que é um comprimido de liberação prolongada.
Depois de uma grande retirada do intestino delgado, remédios de liberação prolongada costumam ser evitados. Eles precisam de um trajeto longo e normal no intestino para soltar o remédio.
Com o intestino mais curto ou um trânsito rápido, parte da dose pode sair do corpo antes de ser liberada.
Produtos de liberação lenta podem soltar parte da dose no intestino grosso. Sem o cólon, eles têm menos tempo e menos superfície para isso.
A absorção muda de remédio para remédio. Por isso, cada um deve ser avaliado em separado com o médico ou o farmacêutico. Seu médico conhece o seu caso, e a decisão é dele junto com você.
O rótulo diz que este comprimido deve ser engolido inteiro, sem partir, mastigar nem triturar. Qualquer mudança na forma de tomar é uma decisão do seu farmacêutico ou médico.
Se o remédio parecer não fazer o efeito esperado, pode ser falta de absorção. Isso deve ser levado ao médico ou ao farmacêutico.
Uma versão de liberação imediata ou líquida do mesmo remédio costuma ser uma boa pergunta para o farmacêutico.
Ninguém com a sua anatomia registrou experiência com este remédio na comunidade.

why.claim: This is an extended-release tablet.
The label says the tablet has an enteric coat that does not dissolve in the stomach.
The label says to swallow it whole with liquid, and not to chew, divide or crush it.
After a large small-bowel resection, guidelines generally avoid slow-release and coated medicines. These designs need a long, normal trip through the gut to release the drug.
When the bowel is shorter or moves faster, part of a time-release dose may leave the body before it is released.
With fast transit, a coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets pass through whole.
How well pills are absorbed depends more on how much healthy small bowel is left than on the type of stoma.
Guidelines say an immediate-release or liquid version of the same drug is often worth asking the pharmacist about.
Liquid medicines may be absorbed more reliably, but they often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.

evidence.L:boxed_warning: WARNING: LIFE THREATENING ADVERSE REACTIONS Hepatotoxicity General Population: Hepatic failure resulting in fatalities has occurred in patients receiving valproate and its derivatives. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment. Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent intervals thereafter, especially during the first six months [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Children under the age of two years are at a considerably increased risk of developing fatal hepatotoxicity, especially those on multiple anticonvulsants, those with congenital metabolic disorders, those with severe seizure disorders accompanied by mental retardation, and those with organic brain disease. When Depakote Sprinkle Capsules are used in this patient group, they should be used with extreme caution and as a sole agent. The benefits of therapy should be weighed against the risks. The incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases considerably in progressively older patient groups. Patients with Mitochondrial Disease: There is an increased risk of valproate-induced acute liver failure and resultant deaths in patients with hereditary neurometabolic syndromes caused by DNA mutations of the mitochondrial DNA Polymerase γ (POLG) gene (e.g. , Alpers Huttenlocher Syndrome). Depakote Sprinkle Capsules is contraindicated in patients known to have mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder [see Contraindications ( 4 )] . In patients over two years of age who are clinically suspected of having a hereditary mitochondrial disease, Depakote Sprinkle Capsules should only be used after other anticonvulsants have failed. This older group of patients should be closely monitored during treatment with Depakote Sprinkle Capsules for the development of acute liver injury with regular clinical assessments and serum liver testing. POLG mutation screening should be performed in accordance with current clinical practice [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Fetal Risk Valproate can cause major congenital malformations, particularly neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida). In addition, valproate can cause decreased IQ scores and neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure. Valproate is therefore contraindicated for prophylaxis of migraine headaches in pregnant women and in women of childbearing potential who are not using effective contraception [see Contraindications ( 4 )] . Valproate should not be used to treat women with epilepsy or bipolar disorder who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. Valproate should not be administered to a woman of childbearing potential unless other medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. In such situations, effective contraception should be used [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 , 5.3 , 5.4 )] . A Medication Guide describing the risks of valproate is available for patients [see Patient Counseling Information ( 17 )] . Pancreatitis Cases of life-threatening pancreatitis have been reported in both children and adults receiving valproate. Some of the cases have been described as hemorrhagic with a rapid progression from initial symptoms to death. Cases have been reported shortly after initial use as well as after several years of use. evidence.L:clinical_pharmacology: 12 CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY 12.1 Mechanism of Action Divalproex sodium dissociates to the valproate ion in the gastrointestinal tract. The mechanisms by which valproate exerts its therapeutic effects have not been established. It has been suggested that its activity in epilepsy is related to increased brain concentrations of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). 12.2 Pharmacodynamics The relationship between plasma concentration and clinical response is not well documented. One contributing factor is the nonlinear, concentration dependent protein binding of valproate which affects the clearance of the drug. Thus, monitoring of total serum valproate may not provide a reliable index of the bioactive valproate species. For example, because the plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent, the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Higher than expected free fractions occur in the elderly, in hyperlipidemic patients, and in patients with hepatic and renal diseases. Epilepsy The therapeutic range in epilepsy is commonly considered to be 50 to 100 mcg/mL of total valproate, although some patients may be controlled with lower or higher plasma concentrations. 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption/Bioavailability Equivalent oral doses of Depakote (divalproex sodium) products and valproic acid capsules deliver equivalent quantities of valproate ion systemically. Although the rate of valproate ion absorption may vary with the formulation administered (liquid, solid, or sprinkle), conditions of use (e.g., fasting or postprandial) and the method of administration (e.g., whether the contents of the capsule are sprinkled on food or the capsule is taken intact), these differences should be of minor clinical importance under the steady state conditions achieved in chronic use in the treatment of epilepsy. However, it is possible that differences among the various valproate products in T max and C max could be important upon initiation of treatment. For example, in single dose studies, the effect of feeding had a greater influence on the rate of absorption of the tablet (increase in T max from 4 to 8 hours) than on the absorption of the sprinkle capsules (increase in T max from 3.3 to 4.8 hours). While the absorption rate from the G.I. tract and fluctuation in valproate plasma concentrations vary with dosing regimen and formulation, the efficacy of valproate as an anticonvulsant in chronic use is unlikely to be affected. Experience employing dosing regimens from once-a-day to four-times-a-day, as well as studies in primate epilepsy models involving constant rate infusion, indicate that total daily systemic bioavailability (extent of absorption) is the primary determinant of seizure control and that differences in the ratios of plasma peak to trough concentrations between valproate formulations are inconsequential from a practical clinical standpoint. Co-administration of oral valproate products with food and substitution among the various Depakote and valproic acid formulations should cause no clinical problems in the management of patients with epilepsy [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.1 ) ] . Distribution Protein Binding The plasma protein binding of valproate is concentration dependent and the free fraction increases from approximately 10% at 40 mcg/mL to 18.5% at 130 mcg/mL. Protein binding of valproate is reduced in the elderly, in patients with chronic hepatic diseases, in patients with renal impairment, and in the presence of other drugs (e.g., aspirin). Conversely, valproate may displace certain protein-bound drugs (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine, warfarin, and tolbutamide) [see Drug Interactions ( 7 ) for more detailed information on the pharmacokinetic interactions of valproate with other drugs ] . evidence.L:dosage_and_administration: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION Depakote Sprinkle Capsules may be swallowed whole or the contents may be sprinkled on soft food. The drug/food mixture should be swallowed immediately (avoid chewing) ( 2.2 ) Safety of doses above 60 mg/kg/day is not established ( 2.1 , 2.2 ) Complex Partial Seizures: Start at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day to achieve optimal clinical response; if response is not satisfactory, check valproate plasma level; see full prescribing information for conversion to monotherapy ( 2.1 ) Absence Seizures: Start at 15 mg/kg/day, increasing at 1 week intervals by 5 to 10 mg/kg/day until seizure control or limiting side effects ( 2.1 ) 2.1 Epilepsy Depakote Sprinkle Capsules are administered orally. As Depakote dosage is titrated upward, concentrations of clonazepam, diazepam, ethosuximide, lamotrigine, tolbutamide, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and/or phenytoin may be affected [see Drug Interactions ( 7.2 ) ] . Complex Partial Seizures For adults and children 10 years of age or older. Monotherapy (Initial Therapy) Depakote Sprinkle Capsules has not been systematically studied as initial therapy. Patients should initiate therapy at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day. The dosage should be increased by 5 to 10 mg/kg/week to achieve optimal clinical response. Ordinarily, optimal clinical response is achieved at daily doses below 60 mg/kg/day. If satisfactory clinical response has not been achieved, plasma levels should be measured to determine whether or not they are in the usually accepted therapeutic range (50 to 100 mcg/mL). No recommendation regarding the safety of valproate for use at doses above 60 mg/kg/day can be made. The probability of thrombocytopenia increases significantly at total trough valproate plasma concentrations above 110 mcg/mL in females and 135 mcg/mL in males. The benefit of improved seizure control with higher doses should be weighed against the possibility of a greater incidence of adverse reactions. Conversion to Monotherapy Patients should initiate therapy at 10 to 15 mg/kg/day. The dosage should be increased by 5 to 10 mg/kg/week to achieve optimal clinical response. Ordinarily, optimal clinical response is achieved at daily doses below 60 mg/kg/day. If satisfactory clinical response has not been achieved, plasma levels should be measured to determine whether or not they are in the usually accepted therapeutic range (50-100 mcg/mL). No recommendation regarding the safety of valproate for use at doses above 60 mg/kg/day can be made. Concomitant antiepilepsy drug (AED) dosage can ordinarily be reduced by approximately 25% every 2 weeks. This reduction may be started at initiation of Depakote Sprinkle Capsules therapy, or delayed by 1 to 2 weeks if there is a concern that seizures are likely to occur with a reduction. The speed and duration of withdrawal of the concomitant AED can be highly variable, and patients should be monitored closely during this period for increased seizure frequency. Adjunctive Therapy Depakote Sprinkle Capsules may be added to the patient's regimen at a dosage of 10 to 15 mg/kg/day. The dosage may be increased by 5 to 10 mg/kg/week to achieve optimal clinical response. Ordinarily, optimal clinical response is achieved at daily doses below 60 mg/kg/day. If satisfactory clinical response has not been achieved, plasma levels should be measured to determine whether or not they are in the usually accepted therapeutic range (50 to 100 mcg/mL). No recommendation regarding the safety of valproate for use at doses above 60 mg/kg/day can be made. If the total daily dose exceeds 250 mg, it should be given in divided doses. Less than 3% of an administered dose is excreted unchanged in urine. why.claim: This is an extended-release tablet.
The label says to swallow it whole and never crush, cut or chew it.
After a large part of the small bowel is removed, guidelines say sustained-release medicines are generally avoided, because they need a long, normal trip through the gut to release the drug.
With a shorter bowel or fast transit, part of a time-release dose may leave the body before it is released.
Slow-release products may release part of their dose in the large intestine. Your colon is not connected, so they have less time and surface to release.
How well pills are absorbed depends mostly on the length and health of the small bowel that remains.
Your doctor may know things about your body that these sources don't. If your experience differs from the guidelines, that's worth raising with your team, not something I can overrule either way.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#anatomy-groups: Short bowel syndrome is described in three anatomy groups: end-jejunostomy (no colon), jejuno-colic (small bowel joined to part of the colon), and jejuno-ileo-colic (some ileum kept, joined to the colon). Advice on fluids and diet differs between these groups.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#anatomy-residual-length: Remaining small-bowel length bands (for example under 100 cm with an end-jejunostomy) describe risk of needing nutrition or fluid support; they are risk bands, not a line above which everything is safe.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#antimotility: Antimotility medicines (for example loperamide) are a mainstay to slow transit and reduce output; timing relative to meals is set by the care team.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#fluids-ors: A glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the preferred drink to replace fluid and sodium losses in short bowel syndrome, especially with a jejunostomy.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.
evidence.G:pd-2017#hypotonic-jejunostomy: With an end-jejunostomy, plain water, tea, coffee and other low-sodium (hypotonic) drinks can pull sodium into the gut and increase output, so these drinks are usually limited in favor of an oral rehydration solution.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:remane-2025#formulation-classes: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).
evidence.G:remane-2025#patient-education: In the pilot study, 11 of 50 interviewed ostomy patients had seen undissolved medicine, and over 60% said they had not been told how an ostomy can affect their medicines.
evidence.G:sood-2013#ileostomy-dehydration: People with an ileostomy are at higher risk of dehydration and low sodium, and medicines such as diuretics and laxatives can add to that risk.

draft.verdict: I can't tell you to stop or keep taking your aspirin, or what dose to take; that is a decision for your pharmacist or prescriber, but the guidelines flag coated delayed-release tablets for people who have lost a lot of small bowel, and the label couldn't confirm which kind of coating your tablet has.

why.claim: Changing or stopping a medicine, or choosing a dose, is a decision for your pharmacist or prescriber, not for Villi. For plain immediate-release tablets, the guideline itself says choices like crushing are a decision for the pharmacist.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel. Plain immediate-release medicines can often still be absorbed if that part of the bowel is still there.
How well pills are absorbed depends more on how long and healthy the remaining small bowel is than on the type of stoma. Your small-bowel length isn't known.

Enteric-coated and delayed-release tablets are made to get past the stomach before they dissolve. When things move through the gut fast, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some tablets come out whole.
After a lot of small bowel has been removed, delayed-release medicines, including enteric-coated ones, are usually avoided because they need a long, normal gut to release the drug.
The label Villi matched lists the form only as "tablet".
That label's ingredient list names aspirin and hypromellose. The sections that describe the tablet and any coating were missing, so the coating type can't be confirmed.

why.claim: 이 제품은 정제(TABLET)입니다.
라벨의 비활성 성분 목록에는 크레아틴 일수화물과 크로스카멜로스 나트륨이 적혀 있습니다.
먹는 약은 대부분 소장 윗부분(공장 앞부분)에서 흡수되므로, 그 부분이 남아 있으면 일반 즉시 방출 약도 흡수될 수 있는 경우가 많습니다.
먹는 약이 얼마나 잘 흡수되는지는 장루 종류보다 남아 있는 소장의 길이와 상태에 더 좌우됩니다.
빨리 녹는 일반 정제는 장루가 있는 분들에게 녹는 문제 위험이 크지 않은(noncritical) 제형으로 분류됩니다.
회장루가 있는 분은 탈수와 나트륨 부족 위험이 더 높습니다.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#anatomy-groups: Short bowel syndrome is described in three anatomy groups: end-jejunostomy (no colon), jejuno-colic (small bowel joined to part of the colon), and jejuno-ileo-colic (some ileum kept, joined to the colon). Advice on fluids and diet differs between these groups.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#diet-colon-carbohydrate: When the colon is in continuity, complex carbohydrates can be partly salvaged by colonic bacteria, so a diet richer in complex carbohydrates is usually favored for this group.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.
evidence.G:pd-2017#fat: Fat restriction is mainly useful when the colon is in continuity (because of oxalate and fatty-acid effects in the colon); with an end-jejunostomy, fat is an important energy source and is usually not restricted.
evidence.G:pd-2017#hypotonic-colon: Most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is in continuity tolerate ordinary hypotonic fluids such as water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon absorbs water and sodium.
evidence.G:pg139#crushing-immediate-release: For plain immediate-release tablets only, crushing or dissolving may improve absorption in some patients; this is a decision for the pharmacist. Crushing extended-release or enteric-coated products defeats their design and can be dangerous.
evidence.G:pg139#enteric-coating: Enteric-coated and delayed-release products are designed to pass the stomach before dissolving; with rapid transit, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some pass through intact.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#time-release: Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
evidence.G:sood-2013#ask-before-changing-form: Patients should consult a pharmacist before changing the dose form of a medicine, such as crushing, splitting or switching products.
evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: How well oral medicines are absorbed tracks the length and health of the remaining small bowel more than the type of stoma.
evidence.L:pharmacokinetics: The absolute bioavailability of a metformin hydrochloride 500 mg tablet given under fasting conditions is approximately 50% to 60%.

draft.verdict: I can't agree with that: lemonade is usually a sugary drink, and the guidelines say sugary drinks like this are best limited in short bowel syndrome because they can raise stoma output, even if you feel fine right now.

why.claim: Lemonade is usually sweetened. Hypertonic, sugary drinks pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output in short bowel syndrome. The guideline says they are best limited, whatever your anatomy.
Sweetened drinks with a lot of simple sugar draw water into the bowel. They are generally limited in short bowel syndrome.
People with an ileostomy have a higher risk of dehydration and low sodium.

Feeling fine now doesn't rule it out. Watch for thirst, dark urine or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, and stoma output going up. These are warning signs of dehydration, and you should tell your care team quickly if you notice them.
For short bowel syndrome, the preferred drink to replace lost fluid and salt is a glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS).
ORS works because glucose and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel and carry water in with them.
For short bowel syndrome, an ORS with about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium is generally recommended. That is more than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
Typical sports drinks have little sodium and a lot of sugar compared with an ORS for short bowel syndrome. They can't replace it.

why.claim: Typical sports drinks are low in salt and high in sugar compared with a rehydration drink made for short bowel syndrome, so they are not a substitute for it.
A glucose-and-salt oral rehydration solution is the preferred drink for replacing lost fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome.
For short bowel syndrome, the recommended rehydration drinks have about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium. That is more than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
People whose colon is still connected usually handle ordinary fluids like water better than people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon soaks up water and salt.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there. But the type of stoma alone doesn't tell you everything about your gut.
Of 10 people with a colostomy who logged sports drinks, 1 said it helped, 6 noticed no change, and 3 said it made things worse.
Thirst, dark urine or less urine, feeling dizzy when you stand up, and more stoma output are signs of dehydration. Tell your care team quickly if you notice them.

why.claim: How many tablets to take, and when to stop, is a decision for your prescriber or pharmacist. Your prescription label and your pharmacist can tell you what was prescribed for you.
The label lists this as a tablet with an immediate (not slow) release.
Guidelines put plain, fast-dissolving tablets in the lowest-risk group for people with an ostomy. Slow-release and enteric-coated products are the higher-risk ones.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel. Plain immediate-release medicines can often still be absorbed when that part is still there.
How well medicines absorb depends more on how much healthy small bowel is left than on the type of stoma. You have over 200 cm of small bowel.
The label says the tablets can be taken with or without food, but one ingredient (clavulanate) absorbs better with food.
The inactive ingredients listed are colloidal silicon dioxide, ethylcellulose and hypromellose. No sorbitol or other sugar alcohol is listed.
If a medicine doesn't seem to be working, poor absorption is worth raising with your prescriber or pharmacist.

evidence.G:pd-2017#salt: Salting food and choosing salty snacks is commonly encouraged in short bowel syndrome with high output, within the care team's advice for the person's heart and kidney health.

It works because sugar and salt are taken in together through the small bowel, and they pull water in with them. That means the balance of salt and sugar matters.
For short bowel syndrome, rehydration drinks with about 90 to 120 mmol/L of sodium are usually recommended. That is more salt than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.

For comparison, the WHO formula has sodium 75, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L. It was made for sudden diarrhea, and its sodium is below the range usually given for short bowel syndrome.

draft.verdict: I can't give you amounts or a mix-your-own recipe, because how much to drink and how to mix it are for your care team to set, and the WHO formula has less salt than is usually advised for short bowel.

why.claim: A rehydration drink made with sugar and salt is the preferred drink for replacing the fluid and salt you lose with short bowel syndrome.
It works because sugar and salt are taken up together in the small bowel, and they pull water in with them. That means the balance of salt and sugar in the mix matters.

The WHO reduced-osmolarity formula has sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L. It was made for sudden diarrhea. Its sodium is below the range usually given for short bowel syndrome.
For short bowel syndrome, rehydration drinks with sodium of about 90 to 120 mmol/L are usually recommended. That is more salt than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
Drinks with too much sugar pull water into the gut and can raise stoma output. If the sugar in a homemade mix is off, it can make things worse instead of better.
People with an ileostomy are more likely to get dehydrated and run low on sodium.
Thirst, dark urine or less urine, feeling dizzy when you stand up, and rising stoma output are warning signs of dehydration. Tell your care team quickly if you notice them.
Of 14 people with an ileostomy who logged this drink, 7 said it helped, 1 felt no change, and 6 said it made things worse.
Another user said their own dietitian gave them a recipe she had approved.

why.claim: WHO ORS has sodium 75, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L (245 mOsm/L total). It was made for sudden diarrhea, and its sodium is lower than the range usually cited for short bowel syndrome.
For short bowel syndrome, ORS with about 90 to 120 mmol/L sodium is usually recommended. That is more than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
ORS works because glucose and sodium are taken in together in the small bowel, and they carry water with them. So the balance of salt and sugar matters.
A glucose-and-salt ORS is the preferred drink to replace lost fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome.
When your colon is still connected, as yours is, plain drinks like water are usually easier to handle than they are for people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon takes in water and sodium.
If you flavor a home mix, be aware that sorbitol and other sugar alcohols are poorly absorbed, pull water into the gut, and can increase output.
12 people with a colostomy logged ORS: 3 said it helped, 4 said it made no difference, and 5 said it made things worse. These are self-reports, and some are sample data.
Thirst, dark urine or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, and more stoma output are signs of dehydration. Tell your care team quickly if you notice them.

For short bowel syndrome, ORS with about 90 to 120 mmol/L sodium is usually recommended. That is more than many store-bought rehydration drinks have.
ORS works because glucose and sodium are taken in together in the small bowel, and they carry water with them. So the balance of salt and sugar matters.
A glucose-and-salt ORS is the preferred drink to replace lost fluid and salt in short bowel syndrome.

For most people with short bowel syndrome whose colon is still connected, plain drinks like water are usually easier to handle than they are for people with an end-jejunostomy, because the colon takes in water and sodium.

12 people with a colostomy logged ORS: 3 said it helped, 4 said it made no difference, and 5 said it made things worse. These are self-reports, and some are sample data.

swapToAskAbout.text: Ask your care team whether you should use a rehydration drink with the sodium level advised for short bowel, about 90 to 120 mmol/L.

final.verdict: I can't give you an exact number of ounces, because how much to drink is a decision for your care team. Rising output is a warning sign that guidelines say to raise with your care team promptly.

why.claim: Thirst, dark or less urine, dizziness when you stand up, and rising stoma output are warning signs of dehydration. Guidelines say to tell your care team about them promptly.
For short bowel, a rehydration drink with sugar and salt is the preferred way to replace lost fluid and sodium.
For short bowel, the advised sodium level in a rehydration drink is about 90 to 120 mmol/L. That is higher than many store-bought rehydration drinks.
The standard WHO formula has 75 mmol/L of sodium. It was made for sudden diarrhea, and that is below the level usually advised for short bowel.
When the colon is still connected, it absorbs water and sodium. That's why most people with a connected colon handle plain fluids like water better than people with an end-jejunostomy.
Sugary drinks like fruit juice and regular soda pull water into the gut and can make output worse. Guidelines say to limit them.
8 of 12 people with your anatomy (small bowel joined to colon) said a rehydration drink helped. 2 said it made no difference and 2 said it made things worse.

draft.verdict: Je ne peux pas vous donner une quantité par jour : c'est à votre équipe de soins de la fixer, et une stomie qui coule beaucoup est un signe à leur signaler rapidement.

why.claim: La soif, des urines foncées ou plus rares, des vertiges en se levant et une stomie qui coule de plus en plus sont des signes de déshydratation. Il faut en parler vite à votre équipe de soins.
Une solution de réhydratation orale (sucre + sels) est la boisson préférée pour remplacer l'eau et le sel perdus quand l'intestin est court, surtout avec une jéjunostomie.
Pour un intestin court, on recommande en général une solution avec environ 90 à 120 mmol/L de sodium. C'est plus que beaucoup de boissons de réhydratation du commerce.
Avec une jéjunostomie terminale, l'eau, le thé, le café et les autres boissons pauvres en sel peuvent attirer le sel vers l'intestin et faire couler la stomie davantage.
Les boissons sucrées comme les jus de fruits et les sodas attirent l'eau dans l'intestin et peuvent faire couler la stomie davantage.

Votre profil indique une jéjunostomie terminale, mais vous parlez d'iléostomie. Dans les deux cas, le risque de déshydratation et de manque de sel est plus élevé. Ça vaut la peine de vérifier avec votre équipe quelle stomie vous avez.

Parmi les personnes avec une jéjunostomie terminale qui ont noté une solution de réhydratation, 11 sur 15 disent que ça les a aidées et 1 sur 15 que ça leur a fait du mal. Ces notes concernent les solutions en général, pas seulement le Pedialyte.
Un autre utilisateur rapporte que sa propre diététicienne lui a dit que beaucoup de solutions du commerce sont moins salées que celles utilisées pour l'intestin court.

draft.verdict: Whether to stop Horizant or switch to another version is a decision for your pharmacist or prescriber, not one to make on your own. A tablet in your pouch is worth showing them, but it doesn't prove either way whether the medicine is working.

why.claim: A whole tablet or shell in the pouch can mean the medicine didn't dissolve. It can also be an empty shell left after the medicine was released. It's worth showing the pharmacist, but it doesn't prove either way.
Horizant is an extended-release tablet.
The label says to swallow the tablets whole and not to cut, crush or chew them.
Time-release tablets need enough time moving through the small bowel to let out their medicine. With a shorter bowel or fast transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
After a large small-bowel resection, sustained-release medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit.
Without a colon, slow-release products have less time and less surface to release their medicine.
Extended-release products are generally avoided after a large resection. Whether an immediate-release or liquid version of the same medicine could work is a good question for the pharmacist.
Liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols, which can increase output.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms: After extensive small-bowel resection, sustained-release and delayed-release (including enteric-coated) medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal transit to release the drug.
evidence.G:pg139#crushing-immediate-release: For plain immediate-release tablets only, crushing or dissolving may improve absorption in some patients; this is a decision for the pharmacist. Crushing extended-release or enteric-coated products defeats their design and can be dangerous.
evidence.G:pg139#enteric-coating: Enteric-coated and delayed-release products are designed to pass the stomach before dissolving; with rapid transit, the coating may not dissolve in time, and some pass through intact.
evidence.G:pg139#extended-release-avoid: Extended-release products are generally avoided after extensive resection; an immediate-release or liquid version of the same drug is often a question worth asking the pharmacist about.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: Liquid forms may be absorbed more reliably than solid tablets in short bowel syndrome, but liquid medicines often contain sugar alcohols that can increase output.
evidence.G:pg139#time-release: Time-release formulations depend on adequate small-bowel transit time to release their drug; with a shortened bowel or rapid transit, part of the dose may leave the body before it is released.
evidence.G:remane-2025#formulation-classes: Oral formulations can be grouped by dissolution risk in ostomy patients as noncritical (for example solutions and plain fast-dissolving tablets), potentially critical, and critical (for example extended-release and enteric-coated products).

why.claim: Procardia XL is an extended-release tablet.
The tablet has an enteric coating that dissolves as it moves along your gut and then slowly releases the drug.

With fast transit, coated tablets may not dissolve in time, and some come out intact. A shell in the pouch is worth showing your pharmacist. They can help tell whether it is an empty shell or a tablet that didn't dissolve.
Timed-release tablets need enough time in the small bowel to release their drug. With a shorter bowel, part of a dose may leave the body before it is released.
After a large small-bowel resection, sustained-release and coated medicines are generally avoided because they depend on a long, normal gut.
The label says to swallow these tablets whole and not to chew, divide or crush them.
Each medicine changes differently after bowel surgery, so each one should be reviewed with the prescriber or pharmacist.

G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio.text: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel (the first part of the jejunum), so many plain immediate-release drugs can still be absorbed when that segment remains.

final.verdict: Finding a Keppra XR tablet in your pouch is worth showing your pharmacist. It isn't proof either way, and stopping or switching is a decision for your pharmacist or prescriber.

why.claim: A whole tablet or shell in the pouch can mean the medicine didn't dissolve. It can also be an empty shell left behind after the medicine came out. It's worth showing the pharmacist, but it isn't proof either way.
The guideline says patients should talk to a pharmacist before changing the form of a medicine, and that includes switching products.
The label I checked (ELEPSIA XR, a levetiracetam extended-release label used in place of a Keppra XR label) lists it as an extended-release tablet.
For people with an ostomy, extended-release products are in the 'critical' group, the group most at risk of not dissolving properly.
That label says to take the tablet whole and not to split or cut it.
With a colostomy, most of the small bowel is usually still there and medicines are often absorbed normally. But this is not a guarantee.
Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel.
You're not alone: in one study, 11 of 50 people with an ostomy had seen undissolved medicine.
